Most 3D-printed phone docks with "speakers" sound pretty bad. They usually just punch a straight, hollow cone into a block of plastic, which traps the low frequencies and makes your phone sound like it’s playing out of a tin can. I wanted a dock that actually worked, and I wanted it to look like a piece of high-end vintage audio gear on my desk. The Monolith hides a mathematically calculated, 100mm exponential horn inside a solid, minimalist block. Instead of just bouncing sound forward, the internal sweep acts as a true acoustic transformer—just like an old-school gramophone. It physically amplifies the volume and actually brings back the warmth and bass of your phone's speaker without using any electricity. Because phone cases make finding a good dock impossible, I built this to be fully parametric in MakerLab. There's pre-sets for different phones with and without phone cases and I also allow for custom measurements. Just hit the Customize button . Features Fits Your Exact Phone Setup: No more wobbly phones or slots that are too tight. Pick your phone model from the dropdown, then choose your case type (Bare Phone, Slim Case, or Heavy Duty Armor). The customizer calculates the exact tolerances so your phone slides in perfectly. Audiophile vs. Charging Mode: By default, the acoustic chamber is sealed airtight for maximum volume. But if you’d rather use this as an overnight charging dock, just check the "Enable Charging Channel" box. It routes a massive 16mm internal tunnel that easily swallows thick, braided USB-C cables. Supported Device Presets The Monolith's customizer includes precise base dimensions (Width x Thickness) for the following devices. You can select your exact phone model and then pair it with your case type for a perfect fit. Apple iPhone 17 Series iPhone 17 Pro Max: 77.6 mm x 8.3 mm iPhone 17 Pro: 71.5 mm x 8.3 mm iPhone 17: 71.5 mm x 8.0 mm iPhone Air: 74.7 mm x 5.6 mm Apple iPhone 16 Series iPhone 16 Pro Max: 77.6 mm x 8.25 mm iPhone 16 Pro: 71.5 mm x 8.25 mm iPhone 16: 71.6 mm x 7.8 mm Apple iPhone 15 Series iPhone 15 Pro Max: 76.7 mm x 8.25 mm iPhone 15 Pro: 70.6 mm x 8.25 mm iPhone 15: 71.6 mm x 7.8 mm Google Pixel Series (Note: All Pixel presets automatically generate an additional 2.5mm of pocket depth to allow the camera visor to sit flush without snagging). Pixel 10 Pro XL: 76.6 mm x 8.5 mm Pixel 10: 72.2 mm x 8.5 mm Pixel 9 Pro XL: 76.6 mm x 8.5 mm Pixel 9 Pro: 72.0 mm x 8.5 mm Pixel 9: 72.0 mm x 8.5 mm Samsung Galaxy Series Galaxy S26 Ultra: 79.0 mm x 8.6 mm Custom Devices Don't see your phone? Select the Custom option in the dropdown and manually enter your phone's width and thickness! Case Allowances Once you select your phone model, choose your case style. The generator automatically adds the necessary tolerances to your phone's base dimensions: Bare Phone: Adds +0.5 mm clearance for a snug, scratch-free fit. Slim Case: Adds +5.0 mm clearance for standard silicone and leather cases. Heavy Duty Armor: Adds +12.0 mm clearance for rugged, multi-layer cases. Print Instructions (Read Before Slicing!) Supports: OFF. Seriously, do not use supports. If you do, the slicer will fill the internal acoustic chamber with grid plastic, and you will never get it out. The printer will bridge the internal gaps on its own. Infill: 10% Rectilinear is fine. Walls: 2 walls min but 3 walls is default (better acoustics). Denser plastic means less sound bleeds through the sides, forcing all the audio energy out the front bell. Drop a make if you print one, and let me know how it sounds!

Diese modulare Halterung ist die professionelle Lösung für das saubere Trocknen Ihrer bemalten oder mit Airbrush besprühten Modellteile. Das System basiert auf quadratischen und rechteckigen Platten, die mit speziellen, im Lieferumfang enthaltenen Verbindern (Connectors) beliebig erweitert werden können. Ob Sie eine lange Linie, eine T-Form oder sogar um die Ecke bauen möchten – diese Station passt sich Ihrem Arbeitsplatz und Ihren Projekten an. Ein weiterer großer Pluspunkt: Wenn die Halterung gerade nicht benötigt wird, lässt sie sich mit wenigen Handgriffen komplett auseinanderbauen. Die flachen Platten und kleinen Verbinder nehmen im Gegensatz zu klobigen Styroporblöcken so gut wie keinen Platz im Regal oder der Schublade weg. Ein wesentlicher Vorteil ist zudem die Doppelfunktion der Verbinder: 1. Platten verbinden: Um die Station beliebig zu erweitern. 2. Stabilisieren: Wenn keine weitere Platte angeschlossen wird, können die Verbinder als seitliche "Stützbeine" eingesteckt werden. Dies verhindert effektiv, dass die Platte kippt, falls Sie sehr schwere oder große Teile an der gegenüberliegenden Seite zum Trocknen platzieren. Haupteigenschaften: Maximale Modularität: Kombinieren Sie Platten und erweitern Sie diese in absolut jede Richtung. Kompakt & Platzsparend: Nach dem Projekt einfach zerlegen und mühelos verstauen. 4mm System: Kompatibel mit weit verbreiteten 4mm-Stäben (z.B. mit Alligator-Clip-Aufsätzen) oder einfachen Holzspießen. Dichte Lochmatrix: Für maximale Kapazität auf kleinem Raum. Clevere Stabilität: Integrierte Stabilisierungsfunktion durch Connectoren verhindert das Umkippen bei ungleicher Gewichtsverteilung. Druckanweisungen: Material: PLA oder PETG (PETG empfiehlt sich für etwas mehr Flexibilität bei den Verbindern). Infill: min. 8% (Ein höheres Infill sorgt für mehr Eigengewicht und somit für einen noch sichereren Stand). Düsendurchmesser: 0,4mm (Standard). Schichthöhe: 0,2mm. Support: JA, erforderlich. description: Hey everyone, long time no see! Today, I’m introducing my first Cyberbrick creation: the Cyberexcavator. Of course, including its matching remote control. I’ve been eyeing a project like this ever since Cyberbrick was first released. From the very beginning, my plan was to go big and create something truly elaborate. What was also extremely important to me was complete documentation of the entire assembly process. This project is complex and definitely surpasses many other Cyberbrick offerings in its complexity. Nevertheless, everything is explained in such detail in over 100 pages of assembly guide with countless photos, comments, tips, and more that even a dedicated beginner can attempt it! I had always set my sights on an excavator project, but it wasn't until the "Electric Push Rod for Cyberbrick" article was published by Maker Supply, that my ideas finally became feasible. I’ve spent many weeks working on this model - constantly making improvements, printing countless prototypes, going through many spools of filament, and so on. This little excavator handles small stones, sand, and the like with ease, is very precise to control, and of course, it can also pull off the occasional acrobatic maneuver. Here you can see it heading back to where it came from xD. For me, it was exactly the kind of project that’s been "almost finished" for a month and a half, simply because I kept coming up with new ideas! I didn't just want to create a model, but an entire playground - objects that can be interacted with, and so on. I'll tell you a lot more about this model later, but first we have to come to a very important part, which is probably most relevant for most people.: the hardware. To build this model, meaning ONE excavator and ONE remote control including props, you will need the "Cyberbrick Ultimate Hardware Kit ZK003", three "Electric Pushrods PG003", some additional Cyberbrick electronic components, as well as parts such as bearings and screws. To find exactly the items you need, it's best to take a close look at this list (also note the quantities, as some items are needed multiple times): Here, you need to click on „More“ to access the full list. Each thunbnail acts like a link that will guide you to the individual components/kits in the bambu lab store. The desktop version of MakerWorld even has a button that allows you to automatically add all items to your shopping cart - so you don't have to search for everything individually! I tried to keep the number of parts manageable, but this project wouldn't have been possible in this form with the standard kit. What's listed here is precisely what you need to completely recreate the project. The props, which I offer here as a separate profile, naturally don't require any hardware parts and are 100% 3D printed. Though, Not every single part from the Ultimate Hardware Kit is used. So, if you already own some Cyberbrick components, the following list will certainly be helpful to you. I have listed every single component individually here: Article Code Qty. 200mm Servo Extension Cable 3Pin (2PCS) XC011 1 BT2 Socket Head Cap Self Tapping Screws (SHCS) AA193 1 Pack BT3 Socket Head Cap Self Tapping Screws (SHCS) AA112 1 Pack BT3 Socket Head Cap Self Tapping Screws (SHCS) AA108 2 Packs BT3 Socket Head Cap Self Tapping Screws (SHCS) AA201 2 Packs Micro Steel Deep Groove Ball Bearings EA004 5 Packs Wire Pair with SH1.0 IC007 1 030 Micro DC Motor with SH1.0 (2PCS) LA024 2 Packs Dual-axis Plastic Reduction Gear Kit LA017 2 100mm Wire with 2Pin XH2.54 Connectors (2PCS) XC005 2 Packs WS2812 RGB LED with IDC0.8 4PIN (2PCS) KB003 2 Packs Three-Position Rocker Switch Module with 3Pin SH1.0 Connector XA010 1 WS2812 LED Hub with 3Pin SH1.0 Connector (1PCS) XA006 2 14500 7.4V 800mAh Li-ion Battery (1PCS) PC003 4 Momentary Button Module with 2Pin SH1.0 Connector (1PCS) XA008 2 Power Switch Module with 2Pin XH2.54 Connector (1PCS) XA007 4 Dual-Axis Joystick Module with 3Pin SH1.0 Connectors (1PCS) XA011 2 Single-Axis Joystick Module with 3Pin SH1.0 Connector (1PCS) XA009 3 Electric Push Rod PG003 3 Remote Control Transmitter Shield (1PCS) XA005 2 Remote Control Receiver Shield (1PCS) XA004 2 Multi-Function Core Board (1PCS) XA003 4 D4x2 mm Round Magnet (20PCS) CA001 2 Packs However, if you don't own any of the parts yet , it is more cost-effective to order according to the official bill of materials that is found in this post. I’ve looked into this closely, so don't go to the trouble of recalculating it yourself :)f Now that we have discussed everything regarding the hardware, we can return to the model and what makes it special. My idea for the "Cyberexcavator" was to have two completely independently controllable sections: a tracked drive unit and a turret with an excavator arm, each equipped with its own receiver. Why? Because this eliminates the need for cables running between the two sections, allowing the turret to rotate continuously without restriction. This was quite a challenge, as I wanted to keep the model as compact as possible so the scale would align reasonably well with the electric push rods. It was difficult because I had to fit a significant amount of electronics into a very tight space. For me, it was out of the question to design a nice-looking exterior shell while the interior was a chaotic mess of cables and components; every single part has a designated spot where it is securely mounted. The exact same applies to the remote control. I originally designed the drive train with TPU tracks. These offer a bit more grip and deliver the best performance for climbing maneuvers. However, the excavator doesn't spin quite as quickly on the spot with them. The increased friction makes it harder for the tracks to slide across the surface, depending on the terrain you're driving on. For this reason—and because I know many people are hesitant to work with TPU, I also designed a PLA track. After quite a few attempts, I created a version that I personally like even better than the TPU one. It allows for very precise and relatively snappy movement. Pivoting on the spot works wonderfully, even on soft surfaces like a sofa, carpet, or similar. The video where I climb onto the A1 Mini with it, features the PLA tracks; it still works very well, though it requires a bit more finesse with the controls :) Here you can take a look at the various prototypes and part versions that were printed to ensure everything is absolutely right! I decided to set up my main print profile with the PLA tracks. You can find the TPU tracks in a separate profile. However, those require different drive sprockets—which you'll also need to print—and these are included in that profile as well. I cover this in more detail in the assembly guide! I personally really like this part—the turntable that sits between the upper and lower sections of the excavator. It is printed "in place." The outer ring has an internal thread that engages with the corresponding pinion gear on a servo later on. Although I have already noted this in the print plate labels, please do not print this part using matte or fiber-reinforced (CF/GF) filaments. This part requires a filament that produces a smooth surface! For all other parts, the choice of material is technically quite flexible. All battery compartments on this model, as well as on the remote control, are magnetic. For the excavator, the entire upper body section is simply removed, which also provides good access to other components if needed. The powertrain battery can be accessed via a small flap in the base plate, which is also designed as a print-in-place part. It’s much the same story with the remote control. Incidentally, I opted against the disposable battery cases included in the "Ultimate Hatdware Kit" and instead installed rechargeable batteries from the "Cyberbrick" range. I feel that disposable batteries have no place in applications like this in 2026, and it pays for itself very quickly in terms of cost, too. I probably spent two days working on the back section of the remote control alone. Batteries are installed on both sides, each powering a transmitter module. It, too, is printed "in place"—essentially in its closed state. This part gives the remote control an even more industrial look, which is exactly what I’m aiming for. If you have large hands, you might curse a bit here and there when plugging in the batteries—like I do—since it’s all pretty tight. But with some light and a little practice, I can manage it in two seconds now. Here are a few examples of the excavator's controls and functions: The general lighting can be adjusted to two levels and, of course, switched off completely to save battery power. To capture that authentic construction site feel, there is naturally a hazard warning light system, as well as a button that sets the front LEDs to run at full power. You only need the left stick to control the tank tracks. With a bit of finesse - which most people will surely pick up quickly, the model handles beautifully and precisely. There is the most to say about controlling the arm and the bucket, and consequently, there are the most controls for them. When pushed up or down, the right main joystick functions to retract or extend the arm as a whole. The three elements at the bottom control the individual parts of the arm independently. The clue is that identical inputs to the transmitter cancel each other out. This means, for example, that one of the arm segments can be "frozen" while operating the main joystick simply by engaging one of the small levers. Here, for instance, you can see how I achieve a fairly authentic-looking "digging motion" by combining the main stick with the small left lever. By combining the main stick and the small middle lever, for example, you can easily create a movement that allows the excavator to lift itself up. That is exactly what I do in the video when climbing onto the A1 Mini. When I play around with the unit, I hardly ever use more than two levers at a time for the arm—that makes the whole thing relatively simple! However, you can also make fine adjustments to the individual arm segments at any time. I hope you now have a good idea of what to expect from this model—but feel free to reach out via the comments if anything is unclear! The full Assembly guide can be found as a PDF in the „Assembly Guide“ section! In conclusion, I would aslo like to say a few things about printing: This project includes some very small parts—such as the printed dowel pins, which are only 2mm wide, used to assemble the excavator arm. It is therefore crucial that your print bed is very clean before printing this model! I used standard PLA for these profiles, but I am confident that most materials would perform well here, depending on your intended use for the model. For home use, PLA is perfectly adequate. If you plan to use the excavator outdoors, you might want to use a material like ASA. However, keep in mind that you may need to scale up the parts to compensate for shrinkage. As I mentioned earlier—and in the assembly instructions— material choice is most critical for the turntable component. It is not necessarily about the base material itself; PLA, PETG, ABS, ASA, pure nylon, and many others would all work well. However, you should absolutely avoid printing this part using a material with a matte or rough surface finish. So, no matte PLA, no CF/GF (carbon or glass fiber), no glow-in-the-dark, and no sparkle filaments. Basically, nothing containing particles or fibers, and nothing with a matte finish. Please make sure to heed this advice! Otherwise, the servo driving the turntable will immediately let you know that it really doesn't appreciate the increased friction! Aside from that, I’d say this is a relatively easy model to print. Yes, it’s a multi-color print involving quite a few color changes, but even on a single-nozzle machine, the print time doesn't increase excessively, because it is already an extensive print anyway. When printing the lower section of the excavator tower or the decor elelents using a single-nozzle printer, you should either choose a color combination where the contrast in brightness isn't too extreme—unlike yellow and black—or increase purge volumes accordingly to prevent color bleed. Here is an example comparison image showing what can happen if insufficient material is purged during a color change, or when two materials with high contrast are used together. Feel free to let me know if you’d like to see a "no-AMS" profile. However, I do think the model loses a lot of its appeal without the multi-color aspect. The two main parts of the remote control—the housing and the faceplate—require a fair amount of support material. That said, almost all the less-than-perfect areas will be completely hidden once the model is assembled. I’m also considering offering a profile that uses a support interface; please let me know if there’s any interest in that. I really enjoy using those materials myself, though I realize it’s still somewhat of a niche practice. Be prepared to invest a fair amount of time if you want to slice this model yourself (starting from the provided STEP file). The model contains various "print-in-place" objects that first need to be isolated using the "Split to Parts" function, and so on. Therefore, if you wish to make any modifications, I recommend using my 3MF files as a starting point.This project includes some very small parts—such as the printed dowel pins, which are only 2mm wide, used to assemble the excavator arm. It is therefore crucial that your print bed is very clean before printing this model! I hope you like the project and have fun building and playing with it. Feel free to let me know if you’d like to see more Cyberbrick projects. However, my main focus—printer accessories—will remain, so don't worry :) Kind regards, Simon, Made In Meidling I

model_name: 1/28 Tweak Station to help remove chassis tweak
description: This is a Tweak Station used to help you remove tweak from your RC 1/28th scale chassis. There are a lot of tweak videos on youtube to show you what tweak is and how to remove it from your chassis, every chassis is slightly differnt in the way this can be achieved. This design was influenced buy a few other designs already out there and by my previous setup board also available here https://makerworld.com/en/models/2449239-1-28-mini-z-setup-board#profileId-2688656 . Usage : Adjust the leveling screws to make the bubble levels in the middle centered which should mean the platform is level, then place the car with the front axel on the pivoting section at the front or the rear depending on your preference, or what you are adjusting, then adjust the car until the front bubble level is centered, which should make the car de tweaked. Required Hardware: 3 x Bubble level inserts 29x10x10mm (I'm using these: https://www.amazon.com.au/dp/B01L4PUVHQ?ref=ppx_yo2ov_dt_b_fed_asin_title ) 5 x Flanged bearings 4x8x3mm (I'm using these: https://www.amazon.com.au/dp/B0CGXF888Y?ref=ppx_yo2ov_dt_b_fed_asin_title&th=1 ) 1 x Carbon fibre rod 57.5-58x4mm Or a 60x4mm steel dowel pin and file it down to size, Amazon stock it but expensive probably cheaper in local hobby shop. As many as needed 4x6mm shims of various thicknesses to space out the floating plate so it wont bind or flop around to much, can be had on Amazon but might be cheaper in local hobbyshop. Assembly: 1. Start by installing the 5 flanged bearings once installed they should sit flush into the face of the print, the fit should be snug but easy to push in or with slight persuation from the back end of a set of tweezers or something else flat pushing on the flanged side of the bearing, try to keep it parallel with the face of the print. 1.1 Push both of the bearings in the main plate in from the back side. 1.2 On the flaoting plate at the back push the bearing in from the back side. 1.3 On the front of the floating plate push both bearings in from the front. 2. To assembled both parts you can line it up as shown below then push the main plate forward and it should just fall into each other, to unassembled requires a similar process in reverse, just be careful it will pull appart with no force just have to line it up, forcing can break the bearing carrier part of the main plate at the front. Thats a bad day. 3. Once the bearings are all in place and the main parts assembled you can slide the shaft in fron the front, just take it easy and use a pair of tweezers to insert the shims if you are using them as you feed the shaft through, the shaft will be captured on both ends by the bubble level inserts so the shaft must fit flush with both bearings it cannot stick out beyond the bearings or the bubble level inserts will not fit. 4. Once the shaft is installed make sure the floating plate can pivot left to right freely and inserts the bubble level inserts very carefully, they need to be lined up perfecly flat at the top of the slots and then pushed in evenly into the slots, if they start going in at an angle they wont fit and could cause damage, better to pop them out again and slide them in flat. The photo below shows the location of the shims if used via the bown arrows, they go in between the floating plate main body and the main plate body. The last step is to screw in the leveling screws, they are designed to be slightly tight the first time you insert them but will free up after that. Don't force it and make sure they are starting on a thread and will go in nicely. Thats it, enjoy.

SmartLid - Smart Sourdough Starter Lid for WECK-jars is a wireless, battery-powered smart sensor lid for monitoring sourdough starter rise, temperature, humidity, and battery status. It is a complete DIY solution designed to monitor the most important parameters of your starter, helping you identify the perfect time for feeding, baking, or refrigeration. Take the guesswork out of your baking and leverage peak yeast activity for consistently better bread! The device operates fully wireless, powered by a rechargeable LiPo battery, and transmits measurements via Wi-Fi using MQTT to your smart home setup. Features Growth Tracking : Measure and understand the rise of your starter (in mm and %). Climate Monitoring : Track temperature and humidity inside the jar environment. Battery Powered : Fully wireless operation with battery voltage logging and status monitoring. Smart Home Integration : Data transmission via Wi-Fi (MQTT) for easy tracking over time. Low-Power Design : Utilizes ESP32 deep sleep to maximize battery life. Required Components Printed Parts Main Sensor Body (Lid) Upper Electronics Cover Upper & Lower Mounting Rings Electronics Microcontroller: DFRobot Beetle ESP32-C6 Mini (DFR1117) Climate Sensor: Compact 4-pin BME280 Distance Sensor: VL53L1X ToF (Time-of-Flight) sensor Battery: 3.7 V LiPo battery (Type 503040) Power/Charging: USB-C female breakout board + USB-C plug Switch: SS-12F15 slide switch (handle length: min. 3 mm) (as there are several variants of some parts, ensure that you chose the correct parts. Please see github for detailed information) Fasteners 5 x M2.5 x 6 mm screws 6 × M2.5 × 16 mm screws Compatible Glass Jars The design is specifically tailored for WECK Rundrand 100 (RR100) jars, including: WECK tapered jar 500/580 ml (WECK 742) WECK tapered jar 750/850 ml (WECK 743) WECK tulip jar 950/1062 ml (WECK 745) WECK tapered jar 900/1000 ml (WECK 908) Using a different jar? Let me know in the comments! (including inner and outer diameter at the top of the jar) If there is enough demand, I will design and upload matching adapter rings. Note: Other WECK jars using the RR100 lid size should fit as well. A sufficiently tall jar is highly recommended so the starter never touches the lid or electronics, even at peak rise! Software & Integration The complete firmware and setup documentation are available on GitHub: sourdough-smartlid The firmware is optimized for the DFRobot Beetle ESP32-C6 and publishes all sensor data natively via MQTT. Data Collection & Visualization To use this project, an MQTT broker is required. Popular solutions include: Brokers: Home Assistant + Mosquitto, ioBroker, Node-RED, OpenHAB, or standalone Mosquitto on a Raspberry Pi/NAS. Dashboards: Home Assistant Dashboards, ioBroker VIS, InfluxDB + Grafana, or custom MQTT dashboards. example of measurement graph (with grafana): How It Works & Configuration The SmartLid replaces the standard glass lid of your WECK jar. The VL53L1X Time-of-Flight sensor measures the exact distance to the starter's surface to calculate the growth percentage. Simultaneously, the BME280 tracks the microclimate. To save power, the ESP32 remains in deep sleep, wakes up at your defined interval, reads the sensors, transmits the data via Wi-Fi, and instantly goes back to sleep. Fully Configurable: Via the firmware, you can easily adjust the measuring intervals, jar height, sensor calibration offsets, and Wi-Fi/MQTT credentials. Battery-Powered Operation The device is designed to operate wirelessly from a rechargeable LiPo battery. During normal use, the ESP32 wakes up only for a short time, reads all sensors, publishes the data via MQTT, and then returns to deep sleep. This greatly reduces power consumption compared to continuous operation. Estimated runtime with 10-minute measurement intervals: at least one week. Printing & Assembly Notes Print Profile: It is highly recommended to use the provided print profile. Material Recommendation: PLA or PETG is recommended. Supports: The two rings should be printed without supports. The main sensor body and upper cover require supports. Make sure to completely clean all support remnants, especially along the continuous outer rim where the parts seal. Tolerances: Screw holes are designed to fit standard calibrations. However, since printers vary, feel free to leave a comment if you run into fitment issues! Assembly: The stack order is: Lower Ring ➔ Main Sensor Body ➔ Upper Electronics Cover ➔ Upper Ring. Detailed step-by-step assembly instructions can be found on GitHub Disclaimer Food Safety Depending on printer type, material, print settings and post-processing, the printed parts cannot be considered food-safe. Avoid direct contact between the Sourdough Monitor and your starter. Use sufficiently tall jars so that the starter cannot reach the electronics. This project is intended as a monitoring lid, not as a food-contact container surface. LiPo Batteries Lithium polymer batteries can present a fire hazard if damaged, short-circuited, improperly charged, or misused. Build and use this project at your own risk. Always use appropriate charging electronics, avoid mechanical damage to the battery, and never leave charging batteries unattended. Do not use damaged, swollen, punctured, or overheated LiPo batteries. General Disclaimer This project is provided as-is without warranty. Assembly and operation are entirely at the user's own risk. description: This is a kumihimo wheel, a thing to help weave friendship braclets, regular braclets or keychains. Works best printed in TPU, but works in PLA too. How to weave? First, grab 4 strings about the same lenght and tie a knot in the middle as shown, then you will have 8 strings in total. Pull the knot through the middle of the wheel, through the biggest hole. description: Because single-hose portable air conditioners create negative pressure when exhausting hot air, warm outside air is drawn into the room through gaps and openings. This eliminates the negative pressure and significantly improves the air conditioner's efficiency. The cooled air is then recirculated within the room, instead of continuously pulling in warm outdoor air. The adapter features a threadless opening for a 140 mm (14 cm) hose and is compatible with the Siguro SGR-AC-C140W . Added several more models. Elbow adapters for the inlet and outlet hoses (to attach at the end for directing the airflow). Added a simple front panel that allows an outlet hose to be connected to the cold-air outlet (for directing cool air into another room), as well as a new similar panel that allows the airflow direction to be changed either directly from the air conditioner or into the cold-air outlet hose, plus sliding shutters to close the openings. Boostez l'admission de votre moteur classique avec ce cornet d'admission (velocity stack) 100% paramétrique ! Conçu initialement pour le standard 40 mm (entraxe 65 mm) des carburateurs légendaires comme les Weber DCOE, Dell'Orto DHLA ou Solex ADDHE (ex: BX Sport, Alfa Romeo, etc.), ce modèle est entièrement modifiable via l'outil de personnalisation MakerLab pour s'adapter à n'importe quel projet . Que vous cherchiez un simple cornet droit pour votre boîte à air ou un design expérimental pour optimiser le flux d'air, tout est à portée de clic. ✨ Fonctionnalités Uniques et Personnalisables Grâce au générateur paramétrique, vous pouvez ajuster absolument toutes les cotes de la pièce sans logiciel de CAO complexe : 📏 Dimensions sur mesure : Modifiez la hauteur totale, le diamètre d'entrée (l'évasement), le diamètre intérieur de la base et l'épaisseur de la paroi. 🔧 Platine adaptable : Ajustez l'entraxe des goujons, le diamètre des trous et l'épaisseur de la platine pour correspondre à vos carburateurs ou corps papillon (ITB). 🌪️ Option "Vortex" (Style TMAX) : Cochez une simple case pour générer des ailettes internes torsadées ! Le générateur sculpte des pales parfaitement plaquées contre la paroi courbe de la trompette pour créer un flux d'air tourbillonnaire. Vous pouvez régler le nombre d'ailettes, leur épaisseur, leur profondeur et leur angle de torsion. ⛳ Option "Dimples" (Effet Balle de Golf) : Activez cette option pour creuser un motif de petites sphères en quinconce sur toute la surface interne. Cet effet aérodynamique est pensé pour perturber la couche limite et améliorer la vitesse des gaz (comme sur une balle de golf !). ⚙️ Paramètres d'Impression Recommandés Pour une utilisation dans le compartiment moteur, le choix du matériau et des paramètres est crucial pour résister à la chaleur et aux hydrocarbures. Matériau : ASA, ABS, PETG ou Nylon-Carbone (PA-CF). Évitez absolument le PLA , qui se déformerait rapidement avec la chaleur du moteur. Orientation : Imprimez la pièce à plat sur sa platine de fixation (côté moteur vers le bas). Hauteur de couche : 0.12 mm ou 0.16 mm maximum pour garantir une surface interne la plus lisse possible (crucial pour le flux d'air). Supports : Normalement inutiles si l'évasement (courbure) n'est pas trop extrême. Si vous activez l'option "Dimples", une ventilation adéquate est recommandée. Remplissage (Infill) : 100% ou un nombre important de murs (Wall loops : 4 à 6) pour garantir la solidité au niveau de la fixation. 🛠️ Assemblage Ce modèle (dans ses dimensions par défaut de 40mm) utilise la visserie M6 standard des carburateurs concernés. N'hésitez pas à partager vos réalisations, vos réglages de Vortex/Dimples, et les véhicules sur lesquels vous avez monté ces cornets dans les commentaires ! Avertissement : Pièce destinée à un usage sur circuit, compétition ou prototypage expérimental. La modification de l'admission peut nécessiter un nouveau réglage de la carburation (gicleurs) ou de la cartographie.

description: Intex to Bestway Threaded Pool Adapter 🎯 Scopo del Progetto Questo upgrade permette di installare le tubazioni filettate Intex ad alta portata (tipiche delle pompe a sabbia più potenti) sulle piscine Bestway Power Steel nate originariamente con i restrittivi passanti in gomma liscia da 32 mm. description: Behold! After months of design and testing in my free time, I am finally at a point where I can confidently post these files to the public. This design features a conversion kit for the P365 platform from Sig. This is a “drop-in” conversion kit that features pic rails and a charging handle for easier functionality. The main chassis of this model was designed as one whole piece and then split in half in the slicer so that it can be 3D printed on the split line and then mated together with bolts/screws. This was my design intent as it reduced any chances of failure due to layer adhesion and it seemed to be the strongest print orientation for this project. I have meticulously designed the chassis to clamp onto the front rails on the P365 frame and have also incorporated rear locking plates to keep the beavertail on the frame locked into place. This proved to be difficult because there are two different types of beaver tails that come with the P365 platform so I had to make a version for each one. I then designed a “charging handle” that rests on the slide over the rear sight so you can manipulate the firearm while it’s in the chassis. Last but not least, there is an angled magazine holder included in this design that is specifically meant to clip onto the front pic rail of this chassis. This attachment allows you to store an extra magazine on your kit, and it also serves as a crucial clamping point for the chassis/handgun connection. This specific attachment is not required for the functionality of the conversion kit but you must have something mounted to the front pic rail in order to fully lock the chassis (This will be explained further in the assembly guide). I am releasing three version of this conversion kit; the normal closed version (original), the MLOK version (closed version with added MLOK mounts), and the open version (front opened up). You are able to choose whichever one you like best and you can even mix and match the halves since they are symmetrical. Note: THESE FILES ARE INTENDED ONLY AS ACCESSORY COMPONENTS FOR INSTALLATION ON A LAWFULLY OWNED, COMMERCIALLY MANUFACTURED FIREARM. THEY DO NOT INCLUDE FILES FOR ANY COMPONENT THAT IS LEGALLY CLASSIFIED AS A FIREARM UNDER APPLICABLE LAW. YOU ASSUME ALL RISKS ASSOCIATED WITH THE MANUFACTURE, ASSEMBLY, AND USE OF ANY PRINTED OR FABRICATED COMPONENTS. NONE OF THE INCLUDED MODELS CAN BE ASSEMBLED TO MAKE A FIREARM ON THEIR OWN. YOU ARE RESPONSIBLE FOR COMPLYING WITH ALL OF YOUR LOCAL/FEDERAL LAWS WHEN MAKING THIS. NEVER ASSEMBLE THIS KIT WITH A LOADED FIREARM. Final Thoughts: This was originally a personal project that I wanted to make mainly to improve my CAD skills, but also to see if it was even possible to do with a real firearm. The looks or aesthetics of this design was an afterthought as the main focus was strength and function. I designed and redesigned multiple components of this project over the course of many months and I am very happy with the way it turned out. It’s not 100% “drop-in” as some screws have to be tightened after installing the handgun but it is as close as I could get it without introducing any crazy hardware pieces. Feedback is appreciated, enjoy! model_name: RC Trailer for WPL 1:16. scale model
description: I made this trailer to tow behind my WPL-C24 RC car. It started as a hot glued mess of random prints, and a different failed trailer. I decided I wanted to make my own design, and so this was born. I didn't go with functioning suspension for simplicity sake. That way you don't need to worry about printing fiddly leaf springs, or having to buy extra parts, and if you don't care 100% about scale accuracy, it's a lot more straight forward I've used a pin style hitch again for simplicity, you can just use a long screw or piece of wire to hold it on to the cars hitch. To attach it to a vehicle, it will need a hitch similar to the one I've provided on my rear bumper bar design for the WPL-C24 This version of the trailer uses quite a few m3 screws to hold it together. It was a trade off between ease of printing, and assembly. Depending on the response from this trailer, I'm contemplating redesigning the model to print in fewer parts, so it uses fewer screws, but I might need to think how it goes together. Printing: The model is pretty straight forward to print. PLA has been fine for my versions. Some parts will need supports, like the suspension mount, and around the lip of the trailer tray, but they are minor, and mostly any support scarring is hidden from view. You have the option of printing the tray & fenders from one colour, while printing the chassis & suspensions from a secondary colour. I've separated them onto two seperate plates Parts / BOM As well as the printed parts, you need a couple of other things. A bunch of M3 screws, and some wheels. M3 Button head screws: 4x m3x6mm for fenders 15x m3x8mm for everything else 2x 5mm hex drive wheels with a max diameter of 65mmfrom the likes of a WPL C24 kit, or replacements. 2x m2 screws to hold the wheels on. Assembly: The main assembly is pretty straight forward, screw everything together as pictured. One thing I recommend doing is attaching the hitch swivel first with the screw in the back of the cap. It is easier to do it before you attach the trailer neck to the chassis / tray. The 4 m3x6mm screws are for the fenders. If you use 6mm screws, they will fit perfectly, and not protrude into the model's tray. It's best for clearance to use button head screws for these. The rest of the screws will be the m3x8mm screws. You can get away with using up to 10mm screws for most joints if you have them, apart from the 4x holding the tray to the chassis. These screws also don't need to be button head screws, but for the sake of consistency, that is what I've used. I hope you can enjoy this model. As always, feel free to get in touch if you have suggestions to improve it, or run into issues with printing or assembling it.

Overview The Modular Dive Marker is a fully 3D printable diving marker designed for pools, swimming practice and underwater games. The system consists of a weighted anchor and a floating buoy connected by a rope. Once placed in the water, the anchor sinks to the bottom while the buoy remains visible at the surface, creating a fixed underwater reference point. The anchor can also be used without the buoy as a simple diving target. The design is intentionally modular and easy to customize. An editable STEP file is included, allowing you to modify the model in your preferred CAD software. Features Fully 3D printable Editable STEP file included Modular design User-fillable anchor User-fillable buoy Adjustable rope length (simply tie a new knot) No special hardware required Easy to customize Designed for remixing Anchor The anchor consists of two printed parts. The rope is inserted through the top opening and secured inside the housing with a simple knot that can be accessed through the side opening. The bottom cap unscrews and can be filled with almost any ballast material, for example: Gravel Small stones Stainless steel nuts Screws Fishing weights Aquarium gravel Adjust the ballast amount to match your pool depth and desired stability. The anchor can also be used without the buoy as a standalone diving target for swimming practice and underwater games. Floating Buoy The buoy consists of three printed parts. Its geometry provides enough buoyancy to float on the water surface without requiring any additional foam or flotation material . Simply print the three parts, assemble them and attach the rope. The design is lightweight, durable and easy to customize. Printing Notes ⚠️ Please do not modify the recommended print settings. The anchor body has been intentionally designed without top and bottom solid layers . This allows water to quickly enter the exposed infill structure, preventing trapped air and significantly improving the sinking performance. The visible infill on the top and bottom surfaces is part of the design and not a printing defect . Changing these settings may reduce the anchor's performance and prevent it from sinking as intended. Designed for Customization This project was intentionally designed to be modified. Feel free to create your own versions. Future Buoy Ideas The included buoy is only one possible design. Possible alternatives: Classic buoy Star Heart Diamond Fish Shark fin Turtle Octopus Pirate barrel Treasure chest Lifebuoy Flag Balloon Pumpkin Christmas ornament Ghost Skull Crown Rocket UFO Game Ideas One marker already offers plenty of possibilities: Dive around the marker Retrieve the anchor Underwater navigation Swimming practice Diving challenges Time trials Using multiple markers opens up even more ideas: Obstacle courses Treasure hunts Team relay races Underwater slalom Orientation training Marker collection games Custom diving games Printing Recommended Material PLA PETG (recommended for outdoor use) Supports No supports required. Layer Height 0.20 mm Infill 15–20% Assembly Print all parts. Insert the rope through the anchor. Tie the rope inside the anchor. Fill the anchor with ballast. Screw on the bottom cap. Feed the rope through the bottom part of the buoy . Secure the rope with a knot inside the buoy. Assemble the buoy. Adjust the rope length by tying a new knot inside the anchor if necessary. Included Files Editable STEP file Safety This model is a diving game accessory . It is not a lifesaving or flotation device. Always supervise children around water. Use only in safe swimming environments. Remix This project was designed with customization in mind. Feel free to modify, improve and remix the design. model_name: Mallet Putter - Low Torque / High MOI / Modular
description: Modular High-MOI 3D Printed Putter Looking for a customizable putter without the price tag of today's premium designs? This project combines the flexibility of 3D printing with design features inspired by modern high-performance putters. The putter head is designed to incorporate removable weights, allowing the majority of the mass to be positioned around the perimeter. This increases the moment of inertia (MOI), helping improve stability on off-center strikes while reducing twisting through impact. One of the key features of this design is its modular construction. The shaft insert is a separate component that bolts into the main putter head, allowing different putter head designs to be swapped without needing to remove or reinstall the shaft. Simply remove a few screws, install a new head, and you're ready to go. The shaft insert has a lie angle of 74 degrees and a static loft angle of 3 degrees to match the feel of many center-shafted putters. The design of the head of the putter has been carefully made to ensure that the center of mass is aligned with both the center of the face and the shaft when all weights are inserted. Therefore, the design of this putter naturally eliminates the majority of the torque produced when swinging. This can make it significantly easier to keep the face square at impact. To improve feel, the striking face is printed from TPU, providing a soft but responsive impact that closely resembles the insert faces found on many premium putters. Including the printed parts, added weights, screws, and epoxy, the total mass of the head of the putter is right around 320g. Features High-MOI perimeter-weighted design Center of Mass positioned to produce Low Torque when swinging Modular construction with interchangeable putter heads TPU face insert for a soft, responsive feel Removable shaft adapter secured with screws Designed for commonly available hardware and weights Inexpensive and creative alternative to traditional putters Hope you can have as much fun with this project as I did and get to give it a try out on course! For instructions, materials, and a list of parts to purchase/use, see the information below! Happy printing! Material Selection Body / Shaft Insert - PETG is recommended for outdoor use and to withstand higher temperatures while being relatively easy to print. Face Insert - TPU provides a soft yet confident feel when striking the ball. Assembly Be sure to read all the following steps before beginning assembly of your putter! The order in which some of these steps are taken is very important! Print all required components in your favorite colors. Be sure to print each component in its recommended material. Support removal. This step can be rather difficult due to the way the model must be printed, so my recommendation is to work from the outside inwards. I've used normal supports for the flat-bottomed sections to allow for each of the gaps for the weights to be cleared in a singular piece. Press the TPU face into the putter body. Secure it by using super glue or epoxy. Install the weights. All weights should sit flat within the head of the putter when installed correctly. See the image below for the proper layout of weights. A total of 30 individual 0.25oz weights are to be inserted, with 4 stacked near the face and 2 stacked in all other locations. While removing the film on the weights (making them stick) is recommended, it is not required for the putter to work great. Doing so may reduce noises heard when making contact with the ball slightly but will make it more difficult to remove the weights if interchanging putter heads. Install the bottom plate to the putter head at the 5 holes around the perimeter. Ensure that the side which features cutouts matching the position of the weights is facing the inserted weights. Use 5x M3 x 3/8" wood screws (link provided below for the ones used). Screws should only be hand tight, and do not over-tighten them! Cut down the putter shaft to your desired length (I cut mine down to 36in for my height). For a great step-by-step process to complete this, check out this YouTube video: How to Shorten a Putter with a Steel Shaft . Install the grip to your putter shaft. I recommend completing this step before installing the shaft adapter and putter head as there is less time to work and straighten out the grip in comparison. For a great guide to doing this, check out this other YouTube tutorial: How to Install a Putter Grip (jump to 3:00 in the video). Bolt the shaft adapter/insert into the putter head after sliding the shaft adapter into place from the top. Using 3x M3 x 3/8" wood screws, secure the bottom plate, main body, and adapter together through the bottom in the three central holes. Then, complete the installation by using one more screw in the hole near the top of the putter towards the back. Screws should only be hand tight, and do not over-tighten them! Epoxy the shaft into the adapter by applying epoxy to the shaft and sliding it in from the top. The epoxy which is suggested has a long working time which allows you to rotate the putter shaft so the the grip precisely lines up with its correct orientation. My recommendation for alignment of the grip is as follows: look down the shaft and line up the flat part of the grip with the line on top of the putter which is parallel to the direction of your stroke. Once aligned properly, wipe away any excess epoxy from the top of the putter. Let the putter sit overnight so that the epoxy can fully cure. Next step, rolling putts! Hardware & Non-Printed Parts Required Purchased Components: I've added direct links here so you can source everything needed. Shaft: 0.370in Tip Diameter Straight Stepless Putter Shaft ( Amazon Link ) - $29.95 Grip: Any putter grip should do, but the one seen in all images here is a SuperStroke Zenergy Tour 3.0 ( Amazon Link ) - $34.39 Weights: Important to uses these weights due to their exact size and 1/4oz weight ( Amazon Link ) - $6.99 Screws: M3 x 3/8" Wood Screws ( Amazon Link ) - $6.79 Required Tools/Adhesives: Links are provided in case you may need to get these. If you don't already have some of these, they are also great to have in general for a variety of projects. Epoxy: Simple JB Weld 2-Part Epoxy ( Amazon Link ) - $5.93 Steel Tube Cutter: I used a copper pipe cutter (although it worked, not recommended), but using a proper steel pipe cutter is advised if possible ( Amazon Link ) - $13.99 Total (For Required Components and Printed Parts): ~$80 USD Future Plans This modular platform was designed with expansion in mind. I plan to release additional interchangeable putter head designs that will all use the same shaft adapter, allowing you to experiment with different shapes and weight distributions without building an entirely new putter. If you build one, I'd love to see your make! Feel free to leave feedback or suggestions for future head designs. Happy printing, and good luck on the greens!

more sizes will be available soon / if demand is good :) After looking at normal paintbrushes and thinking, “surely a 3D printer could make one of these,” I ended up making this fully 3D printed working paintbrush. The full brush can print in under 40 minutes , and the best part is that the bristles are replaceable. So if they get too worn, bent, clogged up, or abused during a project, you can just print a fresh set of bristles instead of binning the whole brush. The bristle section is designed to be folded at the 43 mm point so it fits snugly into the brush head. Once fitted, the bristles stick out around 60 mm , but this is very customizable. You can cut them shorter, trim them into shape, or stiffen/soften the feel depending on what you want to use it for. The full brush is around 150 mm long , with the red handle section being roughly 75 mm , making it a short, comfortable, quick-use brush rather than a big chunky tool. This started as a fun “can this be done?” 3D printing idea, but it is actually useful. It could be used as: A quick emergency paintbrush A dusting brush A delicate cleaning brush A model-making brush A small archaeology/excavation-style brush A workshop brush for loose dust or debris Or whatever random use you find for it check oit the pics for assembly help The idea is simple: imagine being somewhere with a 3D printer but no brush. A workshop, research facility, maker space, garage, classroom, campsite, or just your house at midnight when you suddenly need to paint something. Print this, fold the bristles, slot them in, and you have a working brush. No AMS is needed. It can be printed as separate colour parts, or all in one colour if you just want the fastest functional version. Print / Assembly Notes Bristle fold point: 43 mm Bristle length sticking out: around 60 mm Full brush length: around 150 mm Handle grip length: around 75 mm Print time: under 40 minutes AMS: not required To assemble, fold the bristle part at the 43 mm point and fit it snugly into the brush head. You can then trim the bristles to whatever length or stiffness works best for your use. P.S. When folding the bristle part, make sure you fold the shorter end first. One side is longer than the other, and if the longer side is folded the wrong way, it will not fit into the brush head properly. The silver/metal-looking part has been made with general printer tolerances in mind, so depending on your printer, the fit onto the red handle may be slightly loose. A small dab of glue on the inside of the silver part may be needed to hold it securely to the red handle. Once that part is fixed in place, the bristles are still removable and replaceable. Just pull the used bristle section out and fit a fresh one in. You can also trim the bristles to suit your needs — shorter for a stiffer brush, longer for a softer/flickier action.

If you need help, or need the .ino files etc, join our discord: https://discord.gg/fp8gyYxzmE Please test carefully: - calibrate every servo before walking - power the servos from a proper high-current power rail - do not power the servos through the Arduino or small jumper wires - test with the robot lifted before putting it on the ground - start with small movements Parts I used: Arduino UNO Q 12 x Servo A lot Bearings And other basic electronic stuff, as cables, lipos etc… A small note about this project: I know that building such a large quadruped with regular servos does not really make sense from a practical engineering perspective. The servos are limited, the mechanics are not ideal, and there are much better ways to build a serious robot dog. But that was not really the point of this project. I wanted to learn more about robotics, motion control, reinforcement learning, and how AI can be used to train robots. This build gave me a lot of hands-on experience with mechanical design, electronics, servo control, walking patterns, and simulation-based training. For example, I also experimented with training the robot in Godot. This time, I used a different approach: first, I manually designed a walking animation, as shown in video 1. After that, I used PPO training to let the AI improve the movement based on that animation. In video 2, you can see a rendering from the training process. Video 1: Animation done without RL Video 2: Training in Godot 4.5 So even if this robot is not the most practical design, it taught me a lot. My next robot project will combine everything I learned from this build, the training experiments, and all the mistakes along the way. Hallo an alle die den EduColon Kapselautomaten gedruckt haben oder drucken wollen, (übrigens die Fensterteile findet ihr hier: https://makerworld.com/de/models/3020347-3d-window-parts-for-the-educolon-vending-machine#profileId-3393353 ) Mein Upgrade ist passend für: https://makerworld.com/de/models/1646388-remixed-full-vending-machine-200-scale#profileId-1740186 von Naddou oder https://makerworld.com/de/models/1258546-remixed-capsule-holder-for-200-scale-educolon?from=search#profileId-1282437 von Amenthyst3D. Ich habe ihn auch voller Freude gedruckt und musste schnell feststellen, dass ein paar Verbesserungen nötig sind um den Funktionsbereich zu erweitern, die Haltbarkeit des Materials zu verlängern und mehr Coins einwerfen zu können. Als erstes stellte ich fest, dass das innen liegende Fach, welches die Coins auffängt, ein sehr kleines Volumen hat. Die Coins an sich sind ja schon mit fast 5cm im Durchmesser und 6mm dicke recht klobig und groß. So kam es bei uns nahezu immer vor, dass schon nach etwa 5 Münzeinwürfen, der Münzausgang versperrt war. Die Münze blieb dann einfach unten stecken und es verklemmte sich entweder das Drehrad, oder die Münze blieb stecken und drehte einfach durch und fuhr noch einmal mit. Das sah dann so aus: Eine sehr ungünstige Situation, gerade weil ich es für Kinder gedruckt habe und das Drehen immer leichtgängig sein muss. Dreht man dennoch mit Gewalt weiter, so bricht die Mechanik die vom Drehrad gesteuert wird und man muss den Automaten wieder mühevoll auseinander nehmen und das Teil ersetzen. Die andere Option, wenn der Coin mehrfach seine Runden in der Mechanik dreht, ist das ebenfalls blöd, denn jedes Kind möchte ja seine eigene Freude am Münzeinwurf finden. Abgesehen davon, fand ich es auch blöd, dass ich etwa 20-25 Kugeln (5cm) effektiv in den Kugelbehälter einfüllen kann (bei mehr mischt und bewegt es nicht mehr so gut) aber nur etwa 5 Münzen einwerfen kann bevor das System ins stocken gerät. Ich wollte es nicht immer nach 5 Münzen schütteln oder ausleeren. Das macht keinen Spaß. Also öffnete ich den Automaten wieder und überlegte wie ich es Verbessern kann. Dann setzte ich mich an Fusion 360 und fing an meine Gedanken in einen Volumenkörper zu verwandeln. Mein Upgrade löst diese Probleme zuverlässig und beinhaltet: 1) Eine größere Münzauffangschale als Unterbau. Der fertig gedruckte Automat kann einfach auf das zusätzliche Fach drauf gestellt werden. Der Deckel an der Unterseite des Automaten muss geöffnet werden, er wird für diesen Unterbau nicht benötigt und kann bei Seite gelegt werden. In Verbindung mit der größeren Rutsche aus 2) fallen die Coins direkt durchs Loch nach unten in die große Auffangschale. Wie ein Abfluss. So können unendlich viele Coins gesammelt werden, das Volumen ist riesig. 2) Eine größere Rutsche zum nachträglichen Einkleben (doppelseitiges Klebeband reicht schon, oder Sekundenkleber) die einen zuverlässigen und schwungvollen Abgang der Coins gewährleistet und den Ausgang vor dem Steckenbleiben schützt. Die Coins bleiben also nicht mehr am Ausgang liegen und türmen sich dort, sondern bekommen mehr Schwung, um weiter nach hinten direkt durch die Öffnung im Boden zu verschwinden und von der Auffangschale aus 1) aufgefangen zu werden. Die Rutsche ist später von außen nicht mehr sichtbar, die Farbe ist daher unwichtig. 3) Eine Transport- und Ordnungsbox mit Deckel, passend für 20 Coins. Wer mehr Coins verstauen will, kann die Box in der Höhe skalieren. Berechnungsgrundlage ist, dass 1 Coin eine Höhe von 6mm hat. Meine Coins haben einen Durchmesser von 49mm. Sie passieren die Mechanik des Automaten perfekt und passen perfekt in die Box hinein. Jedes Fach kann, dank eines integrierten Schlitzes Coin für Coin geleert werden. Man muss nicht alle zusammen ausschütten. Die Aussparungen für die Coins haben einen Durchmesser von 52mm falls ihr etwas größere Coins habt, passen diese auch. 3 kurze Hinweise zum Drucken: - der Unterbaubehälter besteht aus 2 Teilen, die mit 4 Verbindern zusammengesteckt und an den Kanten geklebt werden müssen. Die Verbinder ermöglichen eine passgenaue Ausrichtung. Der Druck benötigt keine Stützen. - Ihr könnt auch die Füllung reduzieren, damit es schneller druckt (z.B. 5% Infill mit Gyroid, das ist stabil genug) - wartet bis das Druckbett abgekühlt ist, sonst reißt ihr euch die Oberfläche runter. Hier ein direkter Vorher und Nachher Vergleich als GIF: Mit und ohne mein Upgrade: Likes, Kommentare und Bewertungen werden täglich gelesen und beantwortet. Teilt gerne Fotos eurer Drucke. Ich sehe gerne wenn meine Profile zum Leben erweckt werden.

# 🚐 Haltegriff-Upgrade für VW T5 / T6 / T6.1 – Airline-Fitting-Aufnahme & Kleiderhaken Die serienmäßigen Kunststoff-Haltegriffe im Dachhimmel sind konstruktiv nur für kurzes Zugreifen beim Einsteigen ausgelegt – nicht für dauerhaftes Anhängen von Jacken, Handtüchern oder einer quer durch den Bus gespannten Wäscheleine. Genau da setzt dieses Modell an: Es wird **unter den originalen Angstgriff** geschraubt und macht ihn zum vollwertigen Camper-Ausstattungspunkt – **ohne** die eigentliche Haltefunktion einzuschränken, ohne Bohren, ohne Kleben. Ideal für alle, die ihren California, Multivan, Caravelle, Transporter, Kombi, Kasten oder Beach zum echten Reisemobil ausbauen wollen. Mit den Original-Schrauben, in drei Minuten montiert. --- ## ✨ Features - **2× Airline-Bohrungen im Standard-Raster** – nimmt jedes handelsübliche Airline-Fitting direkt auf. Ösen-, Haken-, Ring- oder Karabiner-Fittings werden eingesteckt und verriegelt. Damit lässt sich eine Wäscheleine quer durch den Bus spannen, ein Netz einhängen oder eine schwere Jacke sicher fixieren. - **1× integrierter Kleiderhaken** – für den kleinen Alltagskram: Schlüsselbund, Sonnenbrille, Halstuch, Kappe, leichte Jacke. Immer griffbereit, ohne Zusatzhardware. - **Passgenaue Aussparungen für die Original-Schraubpunkte** – das Teil legt sich sauber um die Fixierpunkte des originalen Angstgriffs. Keine sichtbaren Modifikationen an der Verkleidung. - **Angstgriff-Funktion bleibt 100 % erhalten** – der Griff fühlt sich beim Zugreifen an wie ab Werk. Die Erweiterung wird geräusch- und rüttelfrei zwischen Dachhimmel und Griff eingeklemmt. - **Werkzeugloses Umrüsten** – Airline-Fitting kann jederzeit entnommen oder gewechselt werden (z. B. Ösen-Fitting fürs Wochenende, Haken-Fitting im Alltag). --- ## 🚗 Passend für folgende Fahrzeuge Alle VW T5, T6 und T6.1 in sämtlichen Ausbaustufen: `California` · `California Beach` · `California Ocean` · `California Coast` · `Multivan` · `Multivan PanAmericana` · `Multivan Highline / Comfortline / Trendline / Startline` · `Caravelle` · `Transporter / Kombi / Kasten` · `Shuttle` ⚠️ **Wichtig – zwei Griff-Sub-Typen im T5/T6/T6.1:** - **Version A (dieses Modell):** Passt auf den serienmäßigen Standard-Haltegriff **ohne** bereits integrierten Kleiderhaken (meist im vorderen Fahrzeugbereich verbaut). - **Version B (kommt bei entsprechender Nachfrage separat):** Für den Haltegriff **mit** werkseitig integriertem Kleiderhaken (typischerweise im hinteren Fahrzeugbereich). 👉 Bitte vor dem Druck einen Blick auf euren eigenen Griff werfen. --- ## ⚠️ Materialwahl – bitte unbedingt lesen Dieses Teil wird **im KFZ-Innenraum verbaut** und muss unter zwei Bedingungen zuverlässig funktionieren, die viele Standard-Filamente überfordern: **1. Temperatur im Fahrzeug-Innenraum** Ein VW Bus wird im Sommer hinter der Windschutzscheibe und im Dachhimmel schnell **60 °C und mehr**, in praller Sonne auch deutlich darüber. Filamente, die in diesem Bereich weich werden, verlieren unter Zuglast schlagartig ihre Formstabilität. **2. Mechanische Zugbelastung** Eine nasse Jacke, eine quer gespannte Wäscheleine mit Handtüchern oder ein Karabiner mit dranhängendem Rucksack erzeugen dauerhaft Zugkräfte – genau dort, wo das Filament am heißesten Punkt sitzt. Deshalb bitte **nur folgende Filamente** verwenden: | Filament | Empfehlung | Warum | |---|---|---| | ✅ **ASA** | **empfohlen** | UV-, temperatur- und schlagfest – Standardmaterial für Automotive-Interior | | ✅ **ABS** | empfohlen | Wärmeformbeständig bis ~95 °C, zäh | | ✅ **PA-CF / PET-CF / PAHT-CF / ASA-CF** | Premium-Wahl | Maximale Steifigkeit und Temperaturstabilität, ideal bei dauerhaft eingestecktem Airline-Fitting mit Zuglast | | ⚠️ **PETG** | **nicht empfohlen** | Wird ab ca. 70–80 °C weich (Glasübergang) – im Sommer im Bus grenzwertig, unter Zuglast riskant | | ❌ **PLA / PLA+** | **nicht verwenden** | Wird ab ca. 55–60 °C weich – im geparkten Bus im Sommer garantiert kritisch, Bauteil kann kriechen und versagen | Wer keinen gehärteten Nozzle für CF-Filamente hat: reines ASA reicht für den normalen Camping-Einsatz vollkommen aus. --- ## 🔩 Montage (3 Minuten) 1. Die beiden Torx-Schrauben des Originalgriffs herausdrehen 2. Druckteil **unter den Originalgriff** setzen – die Aussparungen im Druckteil legen sich exakt um die Original-Schraubpunkte 3. Original-Schrauben wieder eindrehen und mit Gefühl anziehen (nicht in den Dachhimmel würgen) 4. Bei Bedarf Airline-Fitting oder Karabiner einstecken – fertig 💡 **Schrauben-Hinweis:** Bei mir haben die **Originalschrauben mit Standard-Länge** einwandfrei gereicht. Sollte durch Fertigungstoleranzen oder Farbabweichung bei euch die Klemmlänge knapp werden: zwei minimal längere Torx-Schrauben mit demselben Gewinde und Kopf aus dem Baumarkt besorgen (typischerweise ~5 mm länger als Original genügt). **Sicherheitshinweis:** Während der Fahrt eingesteckte Airline-Fittings oder Karabiner entfernen – bei einem Unfall besteht sonst Verletzungsgefahr für Insassen. Das gedruckte Teil ist Zubehör für den stehenden Betrieb (Camping, Übernachten, Rangieren im Stand), keine sicherheitsrelevante Komponente. --- ## 📦 Optional erweiterbar mit - **Airline-Fitting deiner Wahl** (25-mm-Raster, EU-Standard): - **Ösen-Fitting** → für Karabiner, Seile, Wäscheleine - **Haken-Fitting** → für schwere Jacken, Handtaschen - **Ring-Fitting** → für Wäscheleine und Gurte gleichzeitig Bezugsquellen: Camper- und Bootsausrüster (Suchbegriff: „Airline Fitting", „Airline Zurrmulde", „Airline Bodenschiene Fitting"). Spirograph This collection of templates represents a comprehensive set of spirographs useful for drawing curves of all kinds. What is a spirograph and how does it work? A spirograph is an instrument used to draw curves called hypotrochoids. It is based on a simple concept: a circumference that rotates in a bigger circumference in a specified ratio. In fact what is important to understand how it works is to know the number of teeth of the bigger wheel, which we call R and the number of teeth of the smaller wheel, which we call r . The nominator of fraction reduced to its lowest terms between R and r tells us the number of petals that our hypotrochoids will have while the denominator, the number of revolutions the smaller wheel will do in the bigger one. The higher the numerator and denominator, the denser hypotrochoids will be, this is likely to happen when the denominator is high and a prime number since it will not be possible to reduce the fraction. How to draw? To draw, you must select and position the large circle (the one with teeth facing inward) in the center of the sheet. Then, choose a small circle (the one with teeth facing outward) and place it inside the large circle so that the teeth mesh. Finally, insert the pen into the desired hole and begin making elliptical movements, trying to follow the path of the small circle while ensuring it never separates from the large one. How to print the model? Each print profile features a wheel R —named after the profile itself—along with smaller wheels r designed to produce a particularly interesting result when combined with that R wheel. You can therefore print the large wheel and any or all of the small wheels included in the print profile. There is nothing to stop you from using small wheels "r" from other print profiles to achieve endless variations. Documentation Before printing, you can view a preview of the designs that can be created using various combinations of large wheels (R) and small wheels (r). This is an example of what you will find in the preview; this way, you can identify a design you like and know exactly which wheel size and which wheel hole to use.

Overview This is a 4x5 Graflok conversion for Polaroid 110A and 110B cameras. You can use this with any standard 4x5 graflok backs - grafmatics, 4x5 120 roll film backs, lomograflok, etc. This has centered framing and full 4x5 coverage. This is an extensive project so please read the full description before proceeding. My goal was to make a high quality, well documented 4X5 conversion for the 110 cameras that worked well, looked good, and was easy to print/assemble. This is far from the first conversion and the previously published versions were invaluable for creating my own take on it. Please check out the list at the bottom for my references and other conversion sources. This is published for non-commercial use. I will be setting up an etsy listing for complete conversion kits if there is demand for it. Camera Selection and Destructive Modification This conversion is ideally suited for the 110B version. It can work on the 110A but the viewfinder will still be obscured. I am working on a potential revision specifically for the 110A. This conversion is destructive and the camera will not be able to be returned to the stock afterwards. Series 40 roll film is long dead and unlikely to ever return but this may still be a deal breaker for some which I understand. The hinges and lens stop will drilled out and removed, the leatherette cut, and two holes enlarged. My camera began as a 110A, but had the rangefinder and top plate from a 900 transplanted over. It has also had the top plate painted and leatherette replaced so it will look different than a typical 110A/900. The rangefinder is not a direct swap, requires drilling and tapping for two fasteners and extensive time calibrating the new rangefinder - I would not recommend this approach for someone without prior extensive repair/calibration experience. If you'd like to know more about the conversion I can write it up here if requested. Tools Required range of small flat and phillips screw drivers hex drivers drill + drill bits magnifying loupe scissors/box cutter Filament Selection ABS-GF is my go-to for the vast majority of things. Durable, not very succeptable to moisture, heat resistant, and has a nice surface finish. The included 3mf file includes my print profile for it, once slowed down I found I get better top surfaces and overall print quality. You need to be careful to get the best bed adhesion as you can and let the parts cool before removing them from the build plate to prevent warp. The tolerances for flatness are very tight for this project and any warp can cause a loss in image quality. The 3mf file orients the parts for the best print orientation and to counteract warp the best I can. Laser Cut Parts The conversion is intended to use the laser cut slide locks. 3D printed versions are available but do not operate as smoothly or securely so while they work, I highly recommend sourcing the slides. I have a few spare sets if you'd like to purchase a prepped set. I personally used Sendcutsend and their design specifications but alternate suppliers are available. The slides should be made from .048" stainless steel, the included step files will not necessarily translate to other materials or thicknessess without adjustment. To purchase upload the included flat pattern step file. The part is too small for their finishing and bending operations without nesting/combining the parts. Once received you'll need to bend the ears (bend line should be 6-7mm from the end), deburr, and file/sand the bearing edge where it contacts the film backs to prevent damage to the backs. Teardown and Preperation Open the rear film chamber to access the inside. Fully tape off the lens and bellows across the film gate to protect them from metal shavings. Drill or dremel off the rivet heads (red) for the hinges on the left side. Peel back the leatherette from the hinge carefully to fully separate the hinge and left door from the camera. Remove the two screws holding the film spool (green). Certain models have rivets through the top and bottom into the body (green arrows), if it is riveted you'll need to carefully drill out and/or pry on the film spool to remove it. After it is removed, drill out the two tapped holes for the screws to 1/8" thru holes. The leatherette over the hinge can be glued back down with contact cement or double sided tape. Drill or dremel off the rivet heads for the right side door. To remove this hinge, you may need to pry it away from the body along the green line using a small pry tool, be careful not to bend or tweak the camera body. Cut the leatherette near the film door latch along the red line. Remove the leatherette to the left of this lineto expose the latch plate and the two hidden fasteners underneath. Remove the four slotted screws retaining the latch plate and keep the screws for later use. If you are omiting the side strap, lift the leatherette on the bottom in this area to acces the hidden strap lug screws and remove lower lug. This area will be covered by the new bottom plate. There is an alternate bottom plate with the cutout for the strap in the files. Before you can add the conversion parts, the rangefinder should be adjusted. Set the focus to infinity and point the camera towards a large object in the distance, perferrably with distinct edges/features you can check against. Adjust the rangefinder mirror screws to correct any misalignment. See guides HERE for 110A or HERE for 110B/900 for top plate removal and rangefinder adjustment screw identification. Reinstall top plate. Drill out the two rivets (red) at the front of the stock lens stop/catch. Remove the two screws (green) to remove infinity stop and keep screws for later. Bill of Material FHSCS = flat head socket cap screw SHCS = socket head cap screw BHCS = button head cap screw Chassis Assembly Chassis Mounting Installed light seal foam between body and conversion chassis - Item 20 Grip and Bottom Plate Installation Alternate grip and bottom plate files are available Graflok Locking Slide Assembly Adjust tension on screws (Item 16) to set slide resistance. Slides can be mounted with the ears facing in or out. Included photos show the slides reversed as it was originally designed but I prefer them mounted as they are shown in the assembly drawings. Final Calibration Once assembled, loosely install the new infinity stop using the original screws. I recommend using a proper ground glass holder or one of the available 3D printable holders like THIS from Apoth. Remember the film plane is not directly against the mounting face of the graflok. If using a piece of DIY ground glass, the ground glass needs to be set back 5mm from the face of the graflok to match the film plane of standard holders. Verify the rangefinder is aligned at infinity, set the camera on a tripod and set up a focus target near by. Focus on the target with the rangefinder, hold the shutter open with a shutter release cable with the aperture wide open. Adjust the position of the lens stop until the focus target is sharp on the ground glass, tighten screws. Check focus accuracy at minimum close focus and at infinity. If the focus is out of wack with the rangefinder, the round rangefinder cam may need further adjustment. References Joao Viegas on Makerworld This was the most direct influence on mine particularly around the graflok mount and spacing from the film place. This is a great option to use standard 2 sided 4x5 film holders and cleverly utilizes a cambo spring back. Morten Kolve at film.kolve.org Fantastic resource with conversion instructions and offers kits for sale. His design has better access particularly for the 110A viewfinder and overall is a more compact design at the tradeoff of off-center framing and not reaching full 4x5 coverage. Albert Cornelissen at cornelissen.me Another great resource, particularly for Lomograflok use. This is a nice compact solution for using the instax back and well documented. Has other published files for replacement top plates as well as his later projects like the MRF2 under the name Identidem Design. Analogue Studio Builder of instax conversions for multiple cameras including roll film polaroids. Super nice guy. Instant Options Builder of 4x5 conversions and a great inspiration for well done conversions
