Adjustable iPad & Tablet Stand Here it is! I'm proud to present to you the new and improved V2 of my adjustable iPad stand. There were lots of things to improve, and I'm happy to say that this is a desk accessory you are going to love. V2 features a dual color design that can be done WITHOUT an AMS, is almost entirely supportless, and on top of that prints in less time than V1. It was almost entirely redesigned from the ground up to optimize strength, functionality, aesthetics, and printability. This stand is perfect for drawing, note-taking, watching videos, reading recipes, or simple to keep your tablet at the ideal viewing angle for you. The friction hinges use printed bolts and hand-tightened knobs, allowing you to easily dial in the perfect resistance without tools. Tighten the knobs for rock-slid support or loosen them slightly for quick angle adjustments. Even lower angles can be achieved by removing the base and just using the arm and main plate. V2, with aesthetics in mind, has an accent color captive insert in the main plate. During the print, the printer has a scheduled pause where you can place the insert into the model before printing resumes, permanently trapping it inside the finished part for a seamless connection, leaving a professional two-colored print without requiring an AMS. For those who prefer a simpler print, I will shortly be publishing a single-color version that prints normally without the pause and insert. So go check that out if you're interested! This print also utilized a unique filament-locked-living-hinge (FLLH) that creates a stable lip far beyond strong enough to support an iPad, or any tablet you choose to put on it. Check the Assembly guide for more details about FLLH assembly. Features • Fully adjustable viewing angle • Strong friction hinges with printed hardware • Tool-free tension adjustment • Captive two-color decorative insert • No AMS required for the two-color version • Integrated Apple Pencil storage • Small storage tray in the base • Clean, modern industrial design • Optimized for easy printing and assembly Printing All structural parts were designed for standard PLA. For best results USE PROVIDED PRINT PROFILE : Prints the bolts and knobs at a finer layer height (0.08) for maximum thread quality and 100% infill for stronger pieces. Pauses automatically at the correct layer for the captive insert placement Assembly Assembly is, for the most part, straightforward, and requires no additional hardware. The most challenging part is the main plate. The print profile should pause all BAMBU LABS printers at the correct layer (layer 15) and you should be able to insert the accent textured plate. The print will then resume and print on top of the insert, sealing it into the print. NOTE: For non-Bambu Labs printers, I suspect you will have to schedule your own pause, or manually pause it, at the correct layer (I don't know *shrug*, I don't own a non-Bambu Labs printer. Let me know it the comments!!!). Once the main plate finishes, you'll need to prepare the filament-locked-living-hinge (FLLH). Crease the print at a right angle along the hinge. The thin layer of filament should fold nicely and make a strong crease. Now, holding the plate and lip folded at 90 degrees, take an 8.5-9in (21.5-22.8cm) strip of filament, preferably the same color as the plate, and thread it through the holes on the plate and lip, which should have lined up perfectly when you folded the piece. Once all the way through, you can either just cut the ends, or heat them with a lighter, and press on them to form a mushroom shape, which will prevent the filament from sliding out. Install the catch in the rectangular hole on the front of the lip, then print and attach the lip brackets (found in the second listed print profile), and the main plate is ready to go! Now just screw in the nuts and bolts and adjust the knob to secure your stand! Notes This design has gone through multiple iterations focused on improving: Hinge strength Thread durability Print reliability Ease of assembly Overall appearance The final version has been tested with an iPad and significantly larger devices and provides excellent holding force while still allowing smooth adjustment with a slight loosening of the knobs. If you enjoy this model, I'd really appreciate a like, rating, or photo of your print! Seeing other people's color combinations is one of the best parts of sharing designs. Happy printing!

description: 64-Slot Large Round Kumihimo disc for round bracelets This is a large round Kumihimo disc featuring 64 slots for strings to make complex high string-count round bracelets with up to 40 strings, using the ancient Japanese artform of Kumihimo , which is done by weaving strings of silk, rope or yarn together using a disc to form a rope/bracelet with artistic patterns in the process. A 64-slot Kumihimo disc is typically used for weaves with more than 16 strings at a time as the complexity of keeping track of the strings increases if they are too densely packed together. The below picture shows the disc with a 24-string pattern using 12 different colors at the same time to create the large pattern. The disc has 64 marked notches to hold the strings in place and allowing to easily make high string-count weaves through the rounded circle slot in the center for the Kumihimo weaving pattern to form. The notches are labelled 1-64 and additionally the notches are marked every 16th slot with a large dot to indicate starting points for 8-string weaves (at16, 32, 48 and 64), as well as every 8th slot in between for 16-string weaves with a smaller circle (at 8,24, 40 and 56), as well as every 4th slot in between the 16- and 8-slot markers for 32-string weaves with a small diamond dot (at 4, 12, 20, 28, 36, 44, 52 and 60). The labels are printed flat on the bed, so the disc is rotated upside down. If using an AMS, the labels are pre-colored and will be printed using a color for the disc and a second for the labels and markings. Without an AMS, the labels will still be visible through the trick of the labels being recessed by one layer height (0.2mm), this embeds the outline of the labels even without color as shown below. If desired, you could trace the etching using a permanent marker after the print. Instructions No assembly is required for the print. Simply print it, get some strings of silk, yarn or rope and you're ready to go. I recommend a string diameter of up to 2mm in thickness (pictured above are a mix of 1mm an 2mm strings). Patterns and instructions on how to use a Kumihimo disc to make rope/bracelets can be found online with several websites dedicated to it and many instructional videos. These aggressive teeth snag and rip through stubborn packing tape instantly. Ergonomic finger ring: Adjust the inner and outer diameter of the ring to fit your finger perfectly. The ring_comfort_radius dynamically generates a smooth, rounded edge on the top of the ring so it does not dig into your skin. Blade profiling: Fully customize the spine curvature, belly curve, and distal taper thickness. Make it a sharp, aggressive claw or a blunt safety opener for kids. Grip grooves: Add tactile ridges (grooves_enable) to the spine where your thumb rests, guaranteeing maximum grip and safety during cutting. 🧠 Behind the design (For makers & moderators) Generating a clean, sharp 3D printed blade without relying on extreme boolean operations or broken meshes requires highly advanced 3D matrix math. This model does not use standard stacked shapes. Instead, it computes an array of 6-point vertex cross-sections that sweep along a dynamically calculated spline ( spine_y and edge_y ). The serrations are mathematically integrated directly into the edge_y array using a phase-biased sine wave algorithm ( tooth_offset ). This means the serrations are not just boolean cuts, but organic curves embedded directly into the mesh structure. The result is a 100% manifold, incredibly clean polyhedron that slices flawlessly and produces a razor-sharp plastic edge right off the build plate. 🖨️ Print settings: Material: PLA Tough, PETG, or ABS/ASA. Standard PLA works, but PETG or PLA Tough is recommended to ensure the tip and serrations do not chip off when hitting heavy cardboard. Layer height: 0.12mm or 0.16mm is highly recommended! Finer layers create a much sharper and cleaner edge bevel. Supports: STRICTLY NONE. The model prints completely flat on its side. Infill: 100% solid or 40% Gyroid. description: ⚠️ Measure your power strip before printing! This is a parametric model. Do NOT print it using the default dimensions unless your power strip matches them. Before generating the model, carefully measure your power strip and enter its dimensions. 1. Add extra length The length of the enclosure should be slightly longer than the actual power strip. Since the power strip is inserted from the top at an angle, it needs some extra clearance during installation. If the enclosure is exactly the same length as the power strip, inserting it will be difficult or even impossible. I recommend adding at least 5 mm (typically 5–8 mm) to the measured length to ensure easy installation. Example: Measured power strip length: 250 mm Enclosure length: 255–258 mm The width and height can remain much closer to the actual dimensions, but the length should always include this additional clearance. 2. Check the cable exit position Before printing, check the distance between the top surface of the power strip and the top of the cable exit (see reference image). This check is important because the power strip is inserted from above. If the cable exits too close to the top of the power strip and your desk is thick, the cable may interfere with the underside of the tabletop during installation. You can verify the required height using this rule: Measure the distance between the top of the power strip and the top of the cable exit . Subtract your desk thickness . Subtract 6 mm (design clearance already accounted for in the model) . Available clearance = (top-to-cable-exit distance) − desk thickness − 6 mm If the result is positive or zero , the default height is sufficient. If the result is negative , increase the model height by that amount (absolute value). Example Top to cable exit: 20 mm Desk thickness: 25 mm Result: 20 − 25 − 6 = −11 mm → Increase height by 11 mm 3. Printing instructions This is a parametric model , meaning you only need to adjust three main values to fit your power strip: Length Width Height Once these values are set, the model will automatically adapt to your specific power strip dimensions. Two-part design The model is split into two separate parts : Top part Bottom part Both parts must be generated using the exact same dimensions to ensure a proper fit. Orientation for printing After exporting the models: The bottom part can be printed as-is. The top part must be rotated 180° before printing to ensure correct orientation and printability + This is necessary due to the geometry of the design. Assembly After printing, the bottom part must be permanently glued to the top part . Once glued, the two parts form a single rigid enclosure ready for installation into the desk. Important note This model was created in Fusion 360 , and while it is fully functional and parametric, this also means there are some design limitations related to the way parameters and exported bodies behave . For this reason, always double-check the exported geometry before slicing. If you follow the steps above, the model should print and assemble without issues. i may try to remodel this in open scad in the future About this model Turn any standard power strip into a clean, recessed desk power outlet. Instead of buying an expensive built-in desk power strip, this parametric model lets you install a regular power strip directly into your desk. Simply customize the dimensions to fit your own power strip, print the enclosure, cut an opening in the tabletop, and press-fit the insert into place. Why I designed this Most recessed desk power strips available online are: expensive available in only a few sizes often made by unknown brands with questionable quality Instead, I bought a high-quality standard power strip from a trusted manufacturer and designed this enclosure to create the same built-in look. The result is: lower cost better electrical quality freedom to choose the power strip you trust a clean and professional-looking installation If you build one, I'd love to see your Make!

description: Comprehensive Guide to the Pocket Mechanical Switch Clicker Fidget 🕹️ Welcome to the ultimate Pocket Mechanical Switch Clicker Fidget project page! This model is specifically engineered for people who love the crisp, tactile sensation of mechanical keyboard switches. It functions as a heavy-duty, portable fidget toy that fits easily into a pocket, backpack, or pencil case. Whether you are trying to stay focused during class, brainstorming your next big project, or just looking for a satisfying way to pass the time, this 3-piece model is the perfect quick print. Key Design Features 💡 100% Support-Free: The geometry of this model utilizes careful bridging angles. You can print the entire file completely flat without generating any waste material. Ultra-Low Filament Consumption: Weighing in at less than 7 grams, you can print dozens of these using leftover filament scraps from the end of your spools. High Interlocking Tolerances: The button caps are designed with a standard cross-stem socket that snugly grabs onto your switches without slipping off during rapid clicking. Technical Print Specifications 🖨️ This model has been sliced and thoroughly tested on Bambu Lab printers to ensure perfect execution. Below is the exact configuration data used during the testing phase. Slicer Parameter Recommended Value Functional Purpose Printer Profile Bambu Lab P1S / X1C Targets standard CoreXY motion systems. Print Bed Type Textured PEI Plate Hides layer lines on the bottom face and improves bed adhesion. Filament Material PLA Basic (Green) Offers rigidity and prevents shrinking or warping. Layer Height 0.24mm Draft Optimizes print time while retaining tight tolerances. Sparse Infill Density 15% Provides a lightweight but structurally sound core. Infill Pattern Grid Ensures equal strength across the X and Y axes. Supports DISABLED (NONE) Eliminates post-processing cleanup and saves material. Wall Loops 2 Layers Keeps outer shells strong enough to withstand heavy finger pressure. Component Dimensional Data 📐 If you plan to modify or scale this project, please refer to the exact millimeter dimensions of the original source files below. Part Name Total Quantity Width (X) Length (Y) Height (Z) Base Part 1 Piece 41.21 mm 42.70 mm 9.00 mm Button Caps 2 Pieces 13.69 mm 17.99 mm 17.30 mm Required Extra Hardware & Materials 🛠️ To turn these plastic parts into a working clicker toy, you will need to source a few external items: Mechanical Keyboard Switches: This model accommodates standard Cherry MX style switches. For the loudest and most tactile click, look for Blue Mechanical Switches (such as dustproof clicky switches found online). “https://www.amazon.com/Zhouwang-Blue-Mechanical-Switches-Dustproof/dp/B0FX2GT2XX/ref=sr_1_3?crid=3IEF9XUEI9D4Q&th=1” 3D Printed Alternative: If you do not have access to real keyboard hardware, you can search MakerWorld for a "3D printed mechanical switch" model and drop it right into the base. Adhesive (Super Glue): Because different brands of switches can vary by fractions of a millimeter, you may need a drop of standard plastic glue or super glue to lock the switches into the housing. Detailed Step-by-Step Assembly Guide 🧩 Follow these instructions carefully to assemble your clicker fidget safely and correctly. Clear the Build Plate: Let your heated print bed cool down entirely before removing the parts. Snapping them off while hot can warp the bottom plate. Examine the Parts: Check the inside of the square switch holes on the Base Part and the cross-shaped slots underneath the Button Caps . Remove any tiny stray plastic strings. Test Fit the Switches: Align your mechanical switches over the two square cavities in the base. Press straight down firmly until the side tabs click into place. Apply Glue If Necessary: If the switches slide out too easily when you pull on them, remove them. Place a tiny drop of super glue onto the inner side walls of the base cavity, then push the switches back in. Let it dry for 5 minutes. Attach the Button Caps: Line up the cross-shaped stem of the switch with the socket under the button cap. Press down evenly until the cap sits flush over the switch body. Frequently Asked Questions & Troubleshooting ❓ What should I do if the button caps are too loose? If your printer over-extrudes slightly, the cross socket might stretch. A tiny piece of paper placed over the switch stem before pressing the cap on will create a tighter fit. Can I print this in PETG or ABS instead of PLA? Yes! If it did, use a small craft knife to carefully scrape the inside edge of the square holes.

Unlike embossed textures, this method produces the appearance of woven carbon fiber directly during printing, creating a clean, premium finish without changing the original model geometry. Simply import the modifier into your slicer, position it over the desired surface, paint the desired area with Fuzzy Skin Painting , then slice and print. ✨ Features Realistic carbon fiber weave appearance Original model geometry remains unchanged Easy to position, rotate, and resize Reusable on multiple models Ideal for electronics cases, automotive accessories, tool organizers, display stands, and decorative parts 📖 How to Use Import your model into Bambu Studio . Add the supplied modifier. Position and scale the modifier over the desired surface. Paint the target area using Fuzzy Skin Painting . Slice and print. 📌 Notes The weave direction can be rotated to match your design. Multiple modifiers can be combined to cover larger surfaces. Only the selected area is affected; the rest of the model remains unchanged. The modifier can be reused on virtually any compatible model. ⚙️ Quick Setup Guide Follow these steps to apply the Carbon Fiber Weave effect. ① Import the Modifier Import your model into Bambu Studio . Add Carbon Fiber Modifier.stl as a Modifier . Position and scale the modifier to cover the desired area. Configure the modifier using the following settings: Fuzzy Skin : None (allow painting) ② Enable Fuzzy Skin Select the model (not the modifier), then go to: Objects → [Your Model] → Others → Fuzzy Skin Configure the following setting: Generator Mode : Displacement Noise Type : Classic Point Distance : 0.1 mm Thickness : 0.1 mm Important: Apply this setting to the model , not to Carbon Fiber Modifier.stl . ③ Paint the Desired Area Select the Fuzzy Skin Painting tool and paint only the surface where you want the carbon fiber weave effect to appear. ④ Slice and Print Slice and print the model as usual. The carbon fiber weave pattern will appear only on the painted area . ❤️ Share Your Prints If you create something using this modifier, I'd love to see your results. This is a no-drill, no-damage organizer that slides over the edge of a shelf, cabinet door, drawer front, or partition and grips it by friction. There is nothing to install — set the panel thickness to match your edge, print, and slide it on. Everything is adjustable in the MakerWorld customizer: - **Panel Fit** — set the exact thickness of the edge you are clamping, plus a grip clearance for an easy slide-on fit. The back lip drops down behind the panel to stop the holder from tipping forward under load. - **Hook** — choose how far the hook reaches out and how tall the upturned lip is so items do not slide off. - **Body** — set the overall width and wall thickness for the strength you need. - **Discrete Hooks** — optionally split the front into several separate hook fingers across the width (great for keys, cables, or utensils) instead of one continuous ledge. The part is a single clean profile, so it generates fast in the customizer and prints flat on its back with no supports. Customization Notes - `panel_thickness` + `grip_clearance` set the clamp gap. Measure your edge and add ~0.4–0.6 mm clearance for a snug slide-on fit; reduce clearance or add a strip of tape for a tighter grip. - `back_drop` longer = more anti-tip leverage for heavier items. - `hook_up = 0` gives a flat shelf instead of a hook. - Enable `split_hooks` and set `hook_count` for multiple separate fingers. - For a non-marring, higher-grip version, print in TPU or line the inside of the clamp with a thin strip of foam tape.

model_name: No-Slip AC Exhaust Hose Window Adapter 150mm
tags: air conditioner|exhaust hose adapter|window seal|portable ac|parametric|customizable|PETG
description: A replacement end piece for the exhaust hose of portable air conditioners that use a 150 mm spiral hose . Unlike most stock end pieces — which only have a couple of short ribs and tend to slip off the hose — this one has a continuous helical thread . You simply screw it on and it stays put. The flat, wide outlet is made to slide through window seal covers (the zip-up "AirLock" type) and into the gap between the open window and the frame. Because it's fully parametric , you can dial it in to your exact hose and window in the Customize panel — no CAD needed. Why you might want this It holds. A real screw thread grips the hose all the way around, so it won't pull out under the weight or movement of the hose. Fits tight windows. Set the slot depth to match your window gap; the wide flat outlet keeps the airflow cross-section up so the AC doesn't choke. Optional retainer ring that wedges the tip behind the seal's zipper so it can't slide back out. Adapts to other hoses. Expose the thread pitch, diameter and direction — works for many 150 mm-class spiral hoses, not just one brand. How to use the Customizer Measure your hose: outer diameter over the spiral ribs, and the pitch (rib-to-rib spacing — easiest is to measure across 5 ribs and divide by 5). Set Hose Outer Diameter , Thread Pitch and Tightening Direction (many AC hoses tighten left / counter-clockwise — check yours). Set Slot Width and Slot Depth to your window. Turn the Retainer Ring on if you want it to lock into the seal zipper. Print a test ring first: set Thread Turns to 1–1.5, print just the collar (a few minutes) and check it screws onto your hose cleanly and in the right direction. Then bump Thread Turns back to 3 and print the full part. Recommended print settings Material: PETG (the exhaust air is warm and the part may sit in sunlight — PLA can soften and sag). 0.2 mm layers (or 0.28 mm for a faster draft — the thread works fine at 0.28). 4–5 walls, ~20–30 % infill, no supports needed (overhangs are shallow). Brim recommended for bed adhesion. The model is already oriented print-ready (flat outlet face on the bed). Compatibility Designed and field-tested for the 150 mm spiral exhaust hose of the Proklima GPC12AN (Bauhaus). The measured hose is Ø ≈ 150.8 mm over the ribs, 16 mm pitch, left-hand. Dark filaments rapidly absorb solar radiation and overheat. * **Sunlight Exposure Limit:** Do not leave the box exposed to direct, intense sunlight for more than **one hour**. Keep it shaded under your side tray, brolly, or inside your carryall when not actively changing rigs to prevent overheating and warping. --- ## 🛠️ Required Hardware & Post-Processing BOM To fully assemble the model with maximum precision, you will need: ### 🔩 Hardware & Consumables: * **Magnets:** 22pcs of `5x2 mm` Neodymium magnets (for tight, secure snap closure and hook alignments). * **Hinge Pins:** 2pcs of `2.6 mm` smooth steel pins. *Hardware Hack:* You can easily source these by pulling the long metal mandrels/pins directly out of standard blind pop-rivets ! Cut to length (~50mm) if necessary. * **Rig Winders:** 3pcs of `67x12 mm` EVA foam winders (with a `17 mm` center hole). * **Adhesive:** Cyanoacrylate (Super Glue) is required to secure the colored accent inlay border line around the perimeter of the lid. ### ⚙️ Precision Post-Processing (Highly Recommended): For a flawless, retail-grade mechanical fit, do not rely purely on raw 3D printed holes. Use these tools to finish the hardware seats: * **For Magnet Seats:** Use a `5 mm` flat-bottom metal end mill (Концевая фреза по металлу) turned gently by hand or at low speed to clean out the magnet pockets. This ensures perfectly flat bottoms and a high-precision, flush press-fit. * **For Hinges:** Run a `2.8 mm` drill bit through the hinge channels before inserting your rivet pins to clear any minor FDM over-extrusion and ensure perfectly smooth, bind-free rotation. --- ## ⚙️ Functional Design Highlights * **Dual-Zone Utility:** Side A features precision layout geometry for immaculate hooklength storage. The branding inlays are modeled at exactly **0.4mm** deep, allowing for incredibly crisp color swaps while preventing river mud or groundbait from packing into deep crevices. * **Rugged Tool Aesthetic:** Features a bold, geometric, chamfered-corner architecture that maximizes structural rigidity and completely resists warping under harsh field conditions. * **Micro-Tolerance Closure:** Designed with tight, crisp hardware mechanical tolerances for a satisfying snap closure that won't accidentally spill inside your bag. --- ## 📊 Verified Slicer Settings This profile has been meticulously dialed in to balance raw part strength with pristine aesthetic text definition: * **Material:** **PETG** or **ASA** is highly recommended for bankside thermal stability. description: 🔧 Parametric Screw‑Lid Container with Partitions — Customizable, Practical, Support‑Free This model is a fully parametric screw‑lid container designed for organization, storage, and everyday utility. Every component — main body , threaded lid , internal partitions , and wall structure — is generated through a synchronized parametric system. Adjust any parameter and the entire model rebuilds instantly with clean geometry and reliable printability. The design is engineered for support‑free printing , smooth threading , and strong structural walls . Whether you're creating a multi‑compartment organizer, a single‑chamber container, or a custom storage solution, this generator delivers consistent, professional results. ✨ What You Can Customize 📏 Main Dimensions Outer Diameter — total width of the container including the lid. Container Height — full height of the base container (excluding the lid). 🧱 Walls & Base Can Wall Thickness — adjust outer wall strength. Lid Wall Thickness — control the lid’s rigidity. Bottom Thickness — set the floor thickness for durability. Optional Rim Height — adds an inner rim for seals, gaskets, or inner lids. 🧵 Screw Lid & Threads Thread Height & Turns — choose how tall the threads are and how many rotations they make. Blunt Thread Cut (%) — removes part of the thread edge for easy lid engagement and no cross‑threading . Smooth Sides — adds a wide band below the threads for smoother lid insertion. Chamfer — clean 45° edges on the lid and base for a professional look and better bed adhesion. 🍰 Internal Partitions (Compartments) Number of Walls — choose how many divider walls you want: 0 = empty container 1 = 2 compartments 2 = 4 compartments 3 = 6 compartments …and so on Partition Wall Thickness — adjust divider strength. 🖨️ Printing & Viewing Options Layout for Printing — place base and lid side‑by‑side or show them assembled. Sectioned View — cut the model in half to inspect wall thickness and thread profile. Part to Print — render the full assembly, base only, or lid only. Print Distance — adjust spacing between parts when laid out for printing. ⚙️ Advanced / Tolerance Parts Gap — default clearance between moving parts (lid vs. threads). Resolution (fn) — Resolution ( fn ) controls how finely curved geometry is tessellated in OpenSCAD. Higher values produce smoother, premium‑quality circular surfaces , but they also increase computational load. When set too high, the model becomes excessively dense, which can slow down rendering significantly and may even lead to render‑timeout errors during preview or export. 🎨 Multi‑Color Export Procedure (Important) When exporting a multi‑part model from OpenSCAD as a 3MF , the file may contain both parts merged into a single object. To prepare it for multi‑color printing in Bambu Studio, the model must be split into separate objects. Procedure Import the generated 3MF file into Bambu Studio. Select the model in the object list or directly on the build plate. Right‑click the model and choose Split → To Objects . Bambu Studio will separate the combined mesh into two independent objects. Assign different colors or filament types to each object, or print them separately as needed. This ensures each part of your SCAD‑generated model can be printed with its own color or material . 💡 Printing Tips Tight Lid? Increase the parts gap slightly (e.g., 0.4 → 0.5). Loose Lid? Decrease the parts gap (e.g., 0.4 → 0.3). No Supports Needed — threads and chamfers are designed for clean FDM printing. Infill — 15–20% Gyroid or Cubic is ideal. Walls — use 3–4 perimeters for extra strength. 🖨️ Print Settings 🧵 Material- PLA, PETG, Matte PLA (matte colors give a premium clean look) 🧱 Infill- 15%–20% Gyroid or Cubic 🧱 Walls- 3–4 walls for strong partitions and thread durability ❤️ Share Your Makes Every print carries a piece of your creativity. Operation Scribe the dovetail cut depth on all workpieces to establish a clear stopping point for each cut. Lay out the tail pattern on one side of a reference board. These layout lines are used to align the jig with the saw blade. Align the first layout line with the blade and make the cut. By flipping the board, the jig produces matching left- and right-hand cuts, ensuring perfect symmetry across all boards. Flip the board end-for-end and repeat the process on the opposite side. Once the first set of cuts is completed, adjust the fence or stop position to the next layout line and repeat until all tails are cut. description: Do you sleep with your hand under the pillow to raise your head, only to wake up with a numb, tingling arm and compressed elbows? The NightMouse is an ergonomic pillow spacer designed to perfectly replace your hand under the pillow, maintaining your preferred sleeping height without cutting off your circulation. Shaped like a symmetrical teardrop, it works intuitively just like a computer mouse: guide it under the pillow with your palm, find the perfect spot, and slide your hand out. To determine the ideal thickness, I measured the maximum thickness of my hand while it was resting completely flat on a table . To get the perfect, tailored fit for your body, I highly recommend doing the same before printing: Place your hand flat on a table and measure its maximum thickness (the height from the table surface to the top of your hand, specifically the area right in front of the wrist ). Check the default thickness of the model in your slicer. If you need to adjust it to match your measurement or personal preference, select the model in your slicer (e.g., Bambu Studio / OrcaSlicer). Give it a quick rub with fine-grit sandpaper to make it perfectly smooth before putting it under your pillow! 💡 How to use the Tissue Version: Fold your tissue in half into a square before sliding it into the slot. description: 🟢STAY GREEN — Automatic Status Presser 😈Passive Aggressive Mode — Passive Aggressive Email Writing Aid Keep your "active" status green. Let the machine handle it. A small 3D-printed desk arm built around an ESP32 and a micro servo. It presses a key on a fixed interval so apps like Teams or Slack keep reading you as active — and if you reposition it over your Caps Lock key instead, it doubles as a passive-aggressive assistant for those emails. ⏱️ Build time: under an hour once printed — minimal supports, no soldering, 3 wires, 2 code uploads, and a 15-minute calibration pass to match it to your own laptop. What It Actually Does Powers on, waits 5 seconds so you can get your laptop positioned, then begins a repeating press-release motion on whatever key sits underneath it Runs on a fixed rhythm: press, hold half a second, release, wait a second, repeat — indefinitely, as long as it's powered Rack-and-pinion arm for a solid, repeatable press Snap-fit printed parts, minimal supports needed Two ways to use it, same firmware both times: Status mode — position it over a harmless key (Shift, Scroll Lock, etc.) near your normal typing area to keep presence status active Passive-aggressive mode — reposition it over Caps Lock instead, and it'll toggle Caps Lock on the same fixed interval while you're away from your keyboard Nothing in the code changes between the two modes — it's the same loop either way, just aimed at a different key. Worth knowing: presses happen on a steady, predictable interval, not randomly, so if you're using passive-aggressive mode expect a metronomic toggle rather than occasional surprise chaos. A quick honesty note: this works by physically pressing a key, not by touching Teams/Slack or your OS, so it won't trip anything network-side. That said, presence status is meant to signal real availability — worth being upfront with your team if you're relying on this daily. 🧰 What You'll Need Electronics 1x ESP32 dev board 1x Bambu Lab micro servo with clutch 3x Dupont wires (male-to-female) Hardware 3x servo screws (usually included with the servo) A small dab of super glue Printed Parts Base, arm, and rack/pinion pieces (STLs attached) — snap-fit, minimal supports Tools Small screwdriver USB cable + computer with Arduino IDE installed USB power bank or wall adapter (for standalone use afterward) 🔧 Assembly — About 15 Minutes 1. Print the parts (not counted in build time) Minimal supports needed. Standard PLA, 0.2mm layers works fine. 2. Snap the frame together Base, upright arm, and rack all snap-fit. Test the rack-and-pinion motion by hand before you glue anything — it should slide smoothly. 3. Mount the servo Seat it in the arm housing, secure with the 3 servo screws. Only add a dab of super glue if a joint feels loose — never glue the gear teeth themselves, they need to move freely. 4. Wire it up (3 connections) Servo Wire ESP32 Pin Signal (orange/yellow) GPIO 18 Power (red) 5V or VIN Ground (brown/black) GND That's the whole circuit — no breadboard, no soldering. 💻 Flashing & Calibration — About 20–30 Minutes Every laptop is a slightly different height and keyboard depth, so this step tunes the arm to your setup. Do this once, and you're done. Step 1: Upload the Calibration sketch Flash the Calibration Code (included below) first — not the main program yet. Step 2: Open Serial Monitor In the Arduino IDE: Tools → Serial Monitor. Set the baud rate dropdown (bottom-right) to 115200 — it has to match Serial.begin(115200) in the code, or you'll see garbled text instead of readable output. Step 3: Position the unit Put the printed unit where it'll actually sit day-to-day, arm roughly over the key you plan to press. Step 4: Find your two angles Type a number from 0–180 into the Serial Monitor input box and hit Enter. The servo jumps to that angle immediately and echoes back: Servo moved to: 80 degrees Sweep through values — try 30, then 90, then narrow in — until you've found: Release angle — arm lifted clear, not touching the key Press angle — arm comes down and fully depresses the key Write both numbers down. A typical pair might be 60 (release) and 85 (press) — yours will differ based on keyboard height. Step 5: Enter your numbers into the Main Code Open the main sketch and drop your two calibrated values into these three spots: void setup() { fingerServo.attach(servoPin, 500, 2400); fingerServo.write(30); // ← your RELEASE angle (starting position) delay(5000); // 5 sec pause to position your laptop } void loop() { fingerServo.write(80); // ← your PRESS angle delay(500); fingerServo.write(60); // ← your RELEASE angle (same value as above) delay(1000); } Use the same release angle in both the setup() line and the loop() — that keeps the arm returning to one consistent resting spot instead of drifting between runs. Step 6: Re-upload and go wireless Flash the updated main code, then unplug from your computer and switch to a USB power bank or wall adapter. It'll run standalone from there. How the Code Works Calibration Code turns your Serial Monitor into a live remote for the servo — type an angle, it moves there and reports back. It exists purely so you can find your two numbers against your real hardware; it's not what runs day-to-day. Main Code is what actually runs once flashed: setup() connects to the servo, moves to the release angle, and waits 5 seconds — your window to slide the laptop into place loop() then repeats forever: press down, hold 0.5s, lift up, wait 1s, press again That's roughly one keypress every 1.5 seconds, nonstop, until it's unplugged. Same code whether it's sitting over Shift for status, or over Caps Lock for chaos — the only thing that changes is where you physically place the arm. Print Settings Minimal supports (small overhangs on the rack/gear area only) 0.2mm layer height Snap-fit tolerances built in — no post-print sanding should be needed Questions or found an issue with the fit? Drop a comment and I'll help troubleshoot.

Membership Want to join an exclusive community and get early access to prints like this one and get commercial sales licenses? Join my membership The Ultimate Players Kit just got a huge upgrade. I've taken quite a bit of community feedback and transformed the Ultimate Players Kit into something truly special: an ancient tome guarding the knowledge of your character. Included is: A leather sculpted exterior No more arachne wheels Stats with included modifiers and saving throws Gold tracker Wider and deeper dice slots Plus it just looks cool as heck Class insignias for decoration Assembly Instructions Assemble the outer cover Using filament for the hinge pins, link the top cover to the spine, then the spine to the bottom cover. Add Connectors to the cover insides Using the included tool, attach the connectors to the insides of the covers. It is important that you add the connectors to the covers first, and not to the tray and tracker inserts. Add the inserts Snap in the tray to the bottom cover, then the tracker frame to the top cover, taking care that the untextured side of them both face into the spine. Add the corner decorations Using a drop or two of CA glue (super glue) or hot glue, affix the corner decorations. The decorations with only one lip goes on the spine side, and the decorations with corner lips go on the outside. Add your insignia I highly recommend using hot glue/hot melt for this. It will make for easier changing when you want to play a new character. Add the lock mechanisms The lock prints with in place supports that need to be removed (see pictures). Once removed, the receiver (the part of the lock without the prongs) gets added to the tray (bottom). Similar to the cover, add the connectors to the lock, then clip the lock to the frame. Be sure to attach the receiver so that the opening faces upwards (towards the clasp) Add the clasp to the tracker frame in a similar fashion to the receiver (connectors into the part, then clip the part to the tracker frame.) Be sure that when adding the clasp, the prongs are facing downwards towards the receiver. Finally, add the decoration to the locks. Build the trackers There are 8 slots for trackers, but only 7 rods. This is intentional, because I have left an open slot for customization in the future. The top half holds the stats, which gets 4 rods, and the bottom half holds skills which get 3 rods. Please see the model photos for which wheels go in which place. I highly recommend using a pick to micro adjust the wheels to get a nice fitment. It is important to note: the panels that cover the wheels are over sized. This is intentional. Because of the print orientation, they have quite a bit of flex allowed and they act as pins to hold the rods in place once assembled. Once all of the tracker wheels are on the rods, it is time to add the panels on top of them. This is the most fiddly, frustrating bit, but take heart: They do fit and it is very satisfying when they do. Print Settings I highly recommend using my print profiles rather than the STLs. I have done a lot of supports painting and speed changed for the metal parts. The wheel geometry has been re-worked so that arachne wall generation is no longer necessary. The covers and spine were designed to be printed standing upwards for optimal resolution of the texture. The rods should be printed with ~30% infill. This is to stop them flexing too much when spanning large gaps. The snap connector holes on the trays do not need supports. The lock mechanism has included supports in the model. A1 Mini Users This is likely going to be a challenging print for A1M. I recommend slowing your printer down and having a super clean plate: washed with hot water and dawn dish soap. Please also monitor your first layer and slow your print speed for the very tall prints. Upgrading from v2/v3 Most of the parts in this one are not compatible with v2/v3. However I took special caution when designing the windows for the wheels to keep them the same size as the previous version because the wheels are the most time intensive parts to print. As such, the wheels from v2/v3 will fit in this version The rods are slightly wider in diameter, so expect a tight fit, but width wise they do work (I have tested it myself.) I do highly recommend printing a new set of wheels however, the inner geometry has been reinforced for a more clicky wheel with less plastic deformation. Special Thanks A huge shout out to ElsnerPepperForge for the thorough beta testing. I could not have produced this without their help.

PLEASE USE THIS MODEL RESPONSIBLY AND ETHICALLY I'm proud to present the most ambitious project I've ever created: the Working Toy Pump-Action Shotgun . This is a 100% 3D printable and capable of firing a harmless projectile using the brand new Working Toy Cartridge V2 instructions (must read before printing!): Before printing: Before starting the print, do a quick automatic calibration of your printer (mainly bed leveling). Make sure the print bed is clean, so that the components do not have adhesion problems. Use the recommended materials. For the springs in particular, it is absolutely necessary to use PETG (translucent PETG is recommended) to ensure proper functioning of the toy (PLA for the springs is not suitable and will not work). Since it is a toy, I recommend printing this model using bright colors , like fuchsia and purple. I'll be more than happy to see what crazy color combinations you can come up with XD, I therefore kindly ask you to post pictures of the printed toy in the comments:) During printing: Make sure the first three layers are printed correctly (serious errors often occur in the first layer). If you use a bed slinger , slow down the print speed to prevent tall components from falling. Check on your printer every now and then to make sure everything is running smoothly. Once the printer is finished, don't remove the components immediately, but wait 5-10 minutes for them to cool . Removing them too quickly will cause slight deformation of the PLA, which could cause problems with the toy's operation. After printing: Gently remove the supports and make sure the brim is completely removed. Some supports require a little more force and patience to remove, even if optimized. For part 26_PLA it is essential, to ensure accurate operation, that the top surface (the green one) that rests on the supports is smooth after their removal. Therefore any remaining support must be removed. Use the following tutorial to assemble the toy. For assembly it is recommended/necessary to use the following tools: Tweezers are required/recommended to insert the filament pieces and remove any supports Superglue is required to glue the parts together as shown in the tutorial Scissors are needed to cut the pieces of filament to the appropriate length Using the toy: Although it is purely a toy, it is necessary to know how to use and handle it correctly. It is strictly forbidden to use this model outside of your private property, even if you use the colored tip (orange/ red ). While I've spent a lot of time designing this toy, it's not perfect , and as a result, malfunctions may occasionally occur . Here's a list of potential malfunctions and possible fixes: In this case, component 6_PLA (it's like a flap), which should lock the second cartridge, fails, causing the second cartridge to also be loaded and thus block the toy from functioning. This error can be caused by several factors, including a defect in component 6_PLA that causes it to be incorrectly bent (due to improper gluing or damage caused during handling), or a problem with the magazine spring, which, if overly tense, pushes the cartridge too hard, eventually bending the part. The solution is to temporarily remove the trigger assembly to bend component 6_PLA slightly inward (therefore towards the opposite), but not too much, so that it can still assume the retracted position during the toy operation. Particular care must be taken not to bend it too much, and especially not to bend it without pressing on the glued section, which, if not done, can cause the glue to fail. This error can be very annoying if the cartridges are loaded, as it often causes the projectile to break inside the barrel. I haven't yet fully clarified the circumstances under which this can happen. The few times it happened to me was when holding the toy tilted too far to the right. If you find this malfunction occurring too often, I'll release a new version of the 26_PLA component (the carrier) that should fix the problem. General maintenance of parts/components Being a plastic toy, this model can break if used too aggressively. Therefore, I recommend handling it with care. Since the model is made of plastic, 3D-printed parts like springs or flaps tend to deform if left under tension for a long time. Therefore, to preserve the correct functioning of the toy as much as possible, it is recommended to remove the trigger group when not playing with the toy, and position the handle as shown in the figure (in partially loaded position). description: This model is a low-power, custom-built toy blaster of my own original design . Ensured to have no internal functionality related to actual complicated gas powered, dangerous mechanisms, methods of modifying them, or inclusion of similar parts or aesthetics. This is strictly a slingshot mechanism , that is tensioned by a lever and connected by snap joints. Functionally and aesthetically, it is the equivalent of a foam dart blaster. All future projects strictly follow these standards, and I will now communicate this directly, not indirectly. — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — [ " Reaper-26" | Lever Action Blaster ] [ Assembly tutorial, More showcases, and rubber band sizes below ] After 4 months of designing and the headache of 100+ reprinted parts from failed tests, I am glad to finally share my hard work here, free of charge, of course. I am finally glad to get this off my back. I will try to upload another model in… 2-3 weeks?…. As long as everything works. This lever action blaster, which I have named the Reaper-26 , is a fully functional toy slingshot powered by rubber bands. I designed this to give a satisfying process of individual round loading and a lever action mechanism that makes handling it a satisfying process, even outside of launching toy bullets. The video below will demonstrate the satisfying clicking sounds the blaster makes when loading. Showcase and Assembly Video: Please watch the last 30 seconds of the video, it contains essential information about how to load it. Improper loading can cause jams and not allow more prop bullets to be inserted. For those who do not have access to YouTube, I am in the process of making an instruction PDF in 2-3 days, these take a lot of effort, almost as much as the video itself. List of features I want to highlight: Individual round loading An internal magazine, that stores fake bullets in the lower barrel. Fake bullet storage on the stock, allowing quick reloads after you empty the internal toy magazine Adjustable and variable rubber band hooks, which I implemented so that many different rubber band diameters can work (I hope this helps with accessibility). The slingshot, magazine, and trigger rubber bands can all be accessed externally without taking the whole thing apart , which is an improvement from my previous model. Unlike traditional bullet launching devices, this toy blaster is 65% more effective because it utilizes the entire projectile, rather than leaving the cartridge to waste. Distance: Averaging from various tests from eye level: 5.0-5.7 Meters 16-18 Feet The launching distance is the same as the my former Deagle. If yours does not reach this distance, then you need stronger bands or they are getting caught and causing friction. Thick rubber bands give more power, please don't use very thin ones. I saw a lot of people do that on my last model… Rubber bands used: Just because I used these exact ones doesn't mean you have to. In fact, these were just lying around my house, so maybe yours could perform even better. The rubber bands attached as part of the Makers Supply are as close to the dimensions as possible. There are no permanent joints, but they are strong enough to where you cannot break them unintentionally. The project is for those seeking a more sophisticated and functional model with many parts. This is a complicated model so these might not be intuitive. Jams or cannot be loaded The projectile slips out when pushing back or unresponsive trigger Weak/no launching -You inserted the toy bullets in a way where they are angled slightly, and they are getting caught on something. When loading, make sure they get straightly positioned and resting on the elevator wall - The magazine tension is too strong (can also cause angled projectiles) - The loading door is not properly going back (The band is weak or broken) and is getting caught - You are not fully moving the lever into place ← too much tension can cause this - You are attempting to load while there is already a projectile in tension - Loading too quickly or aggressively -The trigger tension is too low and cannot hold the projectile in place while it is tensioned, or it does not have enough strength to go back into place -The trigger insert came out a little bit and the transfer bar is uneven. This can also cause an unresponsive trigger -There is already a projectile hidden improperly inside the barrel. Hold the trigger and shake to drop it out (this happens to me) - Way too much slingshot tension -The strength and number of your bands are the biggest factor, thin bands might not be strong enough to fire. - The bands are rubbing against the sides - You just need to add more, ideally you want 4-5 bands that extend to the furthest hook for maximum acceleration - You are not pulling the lever back into place - There is something hidden in the barrel (this happens to me) Also if you ever encounter any jams, removing the rubber bands on the slingshot easily loosens everything up. description: I've created a 90's-style 3D Printer Toy, complete with “Rattle-N-Spin” AMS. I modeled the entire thing in Fusion 360, and spent about a month longer than I'd hoped prototyping. This was a really fun build for me, personally, because I got to do a lot with different types of gears and components that I've never used before in my models, and I learned a ton. The assembly is quite complex, so I put together a detailed Assembly Guide which should make things simpler. A few things to note about this build: This print profile was optimized for a Supertack Cool Plate, and as a result I don't use a lot of brims in my print profile. If you're printing on a PEI plate, I recommend that you download the file and add brims and other supports. This entire model prints at 90% size. The reason for this is I was halfway done modeling when I realized that it wouldn't fit on the build plate. Regardless of your printer size, if you print at 100%, the fasteners and bearings won't fit, so please, only print at 90%. Features: I really tried to capture the feel of a 3d printer and the 90s nostalgia of this style of toy. 3-Axis controls including X- and Y- axis moving print-head plus a Z-axis moving Print Bed! AMS that mimics the “spinning rattles” from 90s plastic toys, as well as some “hit-a-mole" style buttons Visible fat-toothed gears to give the feeling of an old-school STEM toy. Bright colors (of course, you can choose your own colors) Faces and characters that really bring you back. Four “printable” friends: Arty the articulated Dragon, Boaty the benchmark Boat, Scrappy the Scraper, and Eddie Spaghetti. These characters are of course, based on the 4 most common things that folks print on a new 3d printer I should also note that 100% of the modelling for this project was done by me, by hand, using Fusion 360, including the Printable Friends. I hope folks like this!

description: This hex tray is the same exact dimensions as my magnetic hex trays, the only difference is that they are not magnetic and they don't have the outer ribs, everything else is the same. These clips also work to join these trays with my other magnetic trays. The bottom of the clip is super thin so it doesn't raise the trays off the table - be sure to print the clips on a SMOOTH plate. It is a separate print profile. My second set of wireless lit-up dice uses a scifi/cyberpunk theme and is a faster print. Although this isn't a traditional dice tower, it provides a nice thematic mat for dice rolls. In addition to the new base, I have included new dice designs that offer more lighting options. Dice Designs Two basic designs of dice are included - the chart below shows you you can mix and match opaque and translucent filament (along with LED colors) to achieve different effects. The best results are with 0.2mm nozzles so that they numbers can appear sharper. All of these designs rely on a pause in the print to insert the LEDs. Edge-Lit - Red Bambu PLA Translucent Red & PLA Metallic Iridium Gold 0.2mm nozzle 2x Red LED Edge-Lit - Blue Bambu PLA Translucent Blue & PLA Metallic Iridium Gold 0.2mm nozzle 2x Blue LED Edge-Lit - Green Sunlu PLA Translucent Green & Bambu PLA Basic Sunflower Yellow 0.2mm nozzle 2x Green LED Edge-Lit - Dual Color Bambu PLA Translucent Mellow Yellow & PLA Metallic Iridium Gold 0.2mm nozzle 1x Green LED and 1x Red LED Translucent - Blue Bambu PLA Translucent Ice Blue & PLA Matte Dark Blue 0.4mm nozzle (notice the reduce clarity of the numbers) 2x Cool White LED Translucent - White Bambu PLA Translucent Mellow Yellow & PLA Matte Charcoal 0.2mm nozzle 2x Warm White LED Window - Translucent Sunlu PLA Translucent Black & PLA Matte Ivory White 0.2mm nozzle 1x Green LED and 1x Red LED Window - Opaque Gold PLA Metallic Iridium Gold & PLA Matte Ivory White 0.2mm nozzle 1x Green LED and 1x Red LED Window - Opaque Yellow PLA Basic Sunflower Yellow & PLA Matte Ivory White 0.2mm nozzle 1x Green LED and 1x Red LED Light-up Mechanism These LEDs receive their power through a coil in the base. The LEDs themselves can be sensitive to their orientation, position and materials used for printing. This means that they will sometimes land at an angle where the lights are either dim or do not activate as can be see in the GIF below. Dice Balance 3D printed dice are different that traditional ones - they are lighter and feel a bit different when rolling. I was concerned about the weight of the dice (given the added LEDs) so I've made an effort to keep the weight symmetrical. From my brief testing of about 500 rolls, I'm seeing a spread of results that are within the range I see from similar sets of randomized values. Tips & Notes Although the dice can technically be printed with a 0.4mm nozzle, a 0.2mm nozzle provides much sharper results. The colorful COB LEDs compatible with the Induction kit can vary in briskness. I would recommend using the clearest transluscent filament to increase the light that can get through.

In medieval England, not everyone was allowed to build a castle. Instead, you had to apply for a special “ license to crenellate .” Once the permit was granted, you could then add crenellations – those distinctive notches at the top of castle walls – and other fortifying features to your property. This factoid was too delightful for me to ignore so of course I created a bonus fill-in-the-blanks License to Crenellate. Get it now for FREE on my Ko-fi page: https://ko-fi.com/s/4173deb893 🚩 Before You Print 🚩 Just a few common sense things to be aware of: Small parts, choking hazard , keep away from babies/pets/cranky adults This is a miniature and not suitable for everyone Clean build plate is a MUST Textured build plate recommended (high tack plates may break cards upon removal) Fit differs between printers and filaments ; always do a test print before gifting or batch printing. About This castle might look like a fairytale on the surface but it was greatly inspired by real medieval castle architecture. As usual, I did more research than anyone strictly needs to for a tiny pretend castle. I spent a lot of time looking at the battlements which get their tell-tale “this is a castle” look thanks to the crenellations (the slots), the merlons (the “teeth”) and the corbels (the brackets underneath). While I couldn't fit all features that I wanted in this particular castle, I am planning on a larger more-historically accurate kit card which will include such things as a working drawbridge and portcullis. Try not to mix up left and right, or they won't fit! (When in doubt, check the object names in your slicer). Prep Work: Make sure all support material is completely and cleanly removed before assembling. Final Touch: Finish off all low-friction parts with a dab of glue to make the entire model solid. 🧢 The Adihash Rastacap The green, yellow, and red parts of the cap lock together with addet pins. Insert the pins into the arm pieces, then slide on the yellow and red rings in the correct direction, order, and side. Add a dab of glue into the hands and connect them to finish the arms. Glue the completed arms securely into the overall sockets. Slide the shirt piece (with the head attached) into the torso. Necklace: Glue the top tips of the necklace cords under the shirt collar first. Then, glue the other ends into the medallion, and glue the medallion onto the chest pocket. Glue the golden buttons into place to secure them. 🧦 The Socks The red, yellow, and green socks stack vertically over a heavy-duty, tapered structural pin. This single pin anchors everything firmly through the shoes and straight into the overall legs. 👟 The Adihash Sneakers First, slide the black MID part into position underneath the beige BASIS part. Press the green, yellow, and red branding stripes gently into the side slots using some pliers (make sure to keep the order and sides correct!). Original Description ------------------------------------------------------------------------ In the family we have many card games, we like them a lot. Many of these games have their own cases, made of reinforced cardboard or durable plastic. Sometimes, however, the packages are not so good, perhaps they are made of light cardboard and do not have a suitable container to protect the cards. If they then pass into the hands of children, these packages have a short life. I searched a lot among the various designer creations on the web, but often they weren't to my liking or maybe they needed hardware or other accessories to be assembled and I didn't like it. By chance I came across a box that more or less met my needs. The creator, Hugo, whom I thank very much for the work he has done, has made the fusion file with parametric model available. He does not require external accessories for assembly, so no screws, no pieces of filament or no iron wires to cut to size! I downloaded it, made some changes to make it more suitable for my needs (Fillet, Draft etc.), I made a couple of test prints and I realized I had found what I was looking for. It's perfect, my son and my wife approved, so I started creating various boxes of the dimensions we needed, I designed the internal modules to contain the cards and I personalized the lids with the logos of the various games. This one in particular is for the classic UNO game, a game that in my opinion should not be missing from the collection of anyone who loves playing cards. In my profile you will find other customizations and other sizes suitable for the various games we have at home. Good fun ------------------------------------------ In famiglia abbiamo molti giochi di carte, ci piacciono molto. Molti di questi giochi hanno le loro custodie, in cartone rinforzato o in plastica resistente. A volte però le confezioni non sono così valide, magari sono di cartoncino leggero e non hanno un contenitore adatto a proteggere le carte. Se poi passano nelle mani dei bambini queste confezioni hanno vita breve. Ho cercato molto tra le varie creazioni dei designer sul web, ma spesso non erano di mio gradimento o magari avevano bisogno di ferramenta o altri accessori per essere assemblate e la cosa non mi piaceva. Casualmente mi sono imbattuto in una scatola che rispondeva, più o meno, alle mie esigenze. Il creatore, Hugo, che ringrazio tantissimo per il lavoro che ha fatto, ha messo a disposizione il file di fusion con modello parametrico. Non necessita di accessori esterni per l'assemblaggio, quindi niente viti, niente pezzi di filamento o niente fili in ferro da tagliare a misura! L'ho scaricato, ho fatto qualche modifica per renderla più adatta alla mie esigenze (Fillet, Draft ecc..), ho fatto un paio di stampe di test e ho capito di aver trovato quello che cercavo. E' perfetta, mio figlio e mia moglie hanno approvato, così ho iniziato a creare varie scatole delle dimensioni a noi necessarie, ho disegnato i moduli interni per contenere le carte e ho personalizzato i coperchi con i loghi dei vari giochi. Questa in particolare è per il gioco UNO classico, un gioco che secondo me non deve mancare nella collezione di chi ama giocare a carte. Nel mio profilo troverete altre personalizzazioni e altre dimensioni adatte ai vari giochi che abbiamo in casa. Buon divertimento
