description: AMS HT mount X2D/P2S - Standalone and AMS Flipper - V2 This is my brand new and completely (re)built and revamped mount for the AMS HT for X2D/P2S printer frames that can now be used either standalone with the printer by attaching it directly to the printer frame on the back, or with an AMS Flipper from @ Jakob_K_Design attached to the back and integrating with the AMS Flipper handle. The model has been built from the ground up, taking prior experience and designing a fully modular, easy to print frame of the mount that is almost support free for printing, and assembled together using standard hardware forming a strong base for the AMS HT that sits even horizontally with the top of the printer to be side by side with an AMS Pro 2 on top of the printer. The mount can also be extended with the new Filament Track Switch to allow dynamic inputs for the extruders. Core features of the mount The AMS HT mount conveniently sits on the side, flush with the top of the printer, allowing installation of an AMS Pro 2 or other Risers on top of the printer without interference. You can choose between installing the mount directly to the printer frame, or if you are using an AMS Flipper, to the Flipper handle, using the provided compatible bracket. AMS HT mount allowing full view of the side window with minimal obstruction Some highlights of the model: Strong triangular brackets, balancing strength and material use to mount the AMS HT to the side of the X2D/P2S printer frame Full view of the side window below the AMS HT with minimal obstruction Side bracket provides extra strength and vibration dampening from the printer for the front side of the mount Easy to print flat on the bed with no supports needed for the frame and only minimal supports required for the interfacing slots for precision Easy assembly by slotting the four (4) parts of the mount together using standard hardware of M3 screws and square nuts for a strong hold Can either be used: Directly with the printer using the Standalone main bracket or using the AMS Flipper compatible main bracket which slots around the AMS Flipper handle The mount allows access to the l inear rail belt tensioning ports for maintenance The model print profile has been fine tuned for strength, optimizing extrusion settings to maximize strength and limit support interface swaps and harnessing the power of the X2D dual nozzle system. The print profile is optimized to be printed using the X2D using PETG for the frame, with PLA as support interface support layer for crisp results and easy support removal. Note: As the printer frame is shared between the X2D and the P2S, if printing using the P2S, you will have a few nozzle swaps for the interface layers, but they are minimized to just a few, so it shouldn't affect print time dramatically. NOTE: Please be careful with resetting settings, they have been carefully set to have repeatable successful prints and hold to the print bed. Optional Add-on : Designed to be compatible with my X2D Filament Track Switch mount by having a cutout reserved for the mount and utilizing triangles for chord organization. Optional Add-on: Cable organizer using the triangle brackets. Upon request by another user, I designed another add-on to make the cable organization of the 6-pin cable even neater using a figure-8 cable organizer loop that snap-fits into one of the triangle brackets and can be mounted either vertically or horizontally depending on your preference. Hardware required for assembly and installation You will need a few types of M3 Socket Head Screws and thin M3 square nuts: 7x Socket Head Screw M3x30mm (DIN 912) - Bambu Lab store part AA042 x2 3x Socket Head Screw M3x30mm for the mount assembly 4x Socket Head Screw M3x30mm for the installation to the X2D/P2S printer frame 2x Socket Head Screw M3x20mm (DIN 912) - Bambu Lab store part AA040 x1 5x Socket Head Screw M3x10mm (DIN 912) - Bambu Lab store part AA159 x1 10x thin M3 square nuts (DIN 562, ≤2mm height) - Bambu Lab store part AB015 x1 Optional: If you plan to install the Cable organizer you will also need 4x size 8x3mm round magnets (Bambu Lab store part CA008 x1) for the mount in the frame (and another 4x for the organizer itself ) Assembly The assembly is fairly simple and requires just a few standard hardware M3 screws and square nuts, providing a strong hold. You can follow the below step by step instructions, or follow the annotated images for location of screws, nuts and (optional) magnets. As the mount sits right next to the printer frame, for durability the model should be printed using PETG - so dry your filament prior to use! - you want to avoid stringing, warping or lifting off the bed. Print the four (4) parts - To help avoid any warping, you may want to reduce the Aux Fan speed to avoid spot cooling, which can contribute to lifting of large prints, or consider installing an Aux Fan deflector . Print the Main Bracket Pick either the Standalone Main Bracket if you want to install the mount directly to the printer frame or pick the AMS Flipper compatible Main Bracket if you are using the Flipper to mount the bracket to the Flipper Handle Print the Side Bracket for strong support of the mount and provide dampening to limit vibrations from the printer Print the Top Front Mount Bracket that holds the AMS HT and interfaces with the back and side brackets Print the Top Back Mount Bracket that holds the AMS HT and interfaces with the front and main brackets Print optional add-ons as desired: (Optional): Print the Filament Track Switch add-on to mount the Filament Track Switch to the frame over the AMS Flipper Handle and into the AMS HT side mount frame (Optional): Print the Cable Organizer add-on for extra neat organization of the 6-pin cable connecting to the AMS HT Annotated location of mounting hardware: Step by Step instructions: Connect the Top Front and Back brackets through their connecting interface Install two (2) thin M3 square nuts into the inside slots on both left and right side of the top arms Screw two (2 ) socket head screws M3x10mm length from the outside through each of the two arms to connect to the nuts to lock the front and back brackets together Slot the assembled Top Bracket into the Main Bracket through the four trapezoid interface arms note this is a precise interface with 0.15mm tolerances, so check that your printer printed the interfacing arms without any blobs or give them a light sand on the edges as needed Make sure the interface arms are aligned straight and push down using the back of your palm until the top and main brackets are flush - if things are tight and get stuck, a light sideways wiggle can help to loosen things Slot the Side Bracket into the Main Bracket through the two trapezoid interface arms using the same technique Install thin square nuts M3 in all remaining slots, sliding them to their embedded depths: One (1) - Inside of the Top Back bracket One (1) - Upper side of the Top Front bracket Two (2) - Inside of the Side bracket Two (2) - Sunk into the two slots on the back of the Main bracket - use a thin long screwdriver or pliers to push them into place Screw one (1) M3x10mm socket head screw from the bottom of the side bracket through the front bracket , watching until the screw surfaces through the square nut and locks the two parts together Screw two (2) M3x20mm socket head screws from the top of the Main Bracket through the interface arms, meeting the sunk square nuts Screw three (3) M3x30mm socket head screws from the back of the Main Bracket into the remaining holes connecting the Main and Top bracket with one (1) and the Main and Side bracket with two (2) screws (Optional) Install four (4) size 8x3mm round magnets into the holes on the back of the Main Bracket if you plan on installing the optional Cable Organizer. Installation Directly to the printer Remove the four (4) screws from the left backside of the X2D/P2S printer frame Remove the external spool holder mount if it is currently installed at the top and move it tothe bottom of the printer Attach two (2) M3x30mm socket head screws to the top of the mount and two to the bottom of the mounting holes aligning them with the four holes from which you removed the screws Using AMS Flipper Lift the left side (from the back) AMS Flipper Handle up and clip the mount into the handle - this should sit evenly almost flush on both sides -the mount will minimally protrude prior to tightening of the screws to create a counter clamping force to the AMS Flipper Handle to ensure a strong tight fit, but it will still allow the Flipper Handle to sit flush against the printer frame once aligned correctly as pictured below. Lower the Handle onto the printer and align the top and bottom evenly. A small gap before tightening the screws is ok but it should only be 1-2mm and be even between the top and bottom of the handle. If mount was correctly clicked into the handle and the handle sits even as shown above, screw the four (4) M3x30mm socket head screws onto the printer frame. I recommend starting with one of the bottom screws, but without fully tightening it, and then moving to the top and then finishing the rest of the screws and tightening things into place. Check that the flush fit hasn't shifted in case you tightened one screw before alignment was locked into place. The AMS HT mount and the top and bottom of the AMS Flipper handle should sit basically flush with the printer if the AMS HT side mount was clicked into place together correctly once everything is tightened as shown below: If things don't sit flush correctly, repeat Step 1-3, check the fit and try again until the mount is properly set in the center of the handle, resulting in a flush fit. description: I designed this filament storage case to organize a large number of filament spools and make them quick and easy to access. The cases can be stacked vertically and arranged side by side. Because the lid opens from the front, you can remove the filament you need without moving the other cases. The case includes a large clear window, a hygrometer mount, a desiccant compartment, and a TPU gasket. These features make your filament easier to identify, access, and store. I hope this design helps you keep your 3D printing workspace organized and easy to use. I have uploaded a video explaining this model on YouTube: https://youtu.be/SJGec_SRGWo Main Features Access Your Spool Without Moving the Stack The lid opens from the front. Even when several cases are stacked vertically or placed side by side, you can open each case individually without removing the cases above it. This is especially useful when storing a large number of filament spools in a limited space. Large Clear Window The lid has a large clear window. By using a transparent acrylic or PVC sheet, you can check the filament color, remaining amount, and surface texture without opening the case. The lid locking nut can be printed with the same filament stored inside the case. This allows it to be used as a color sample. If you have a label printer, adding labels such as PLA, PETG, ABS, or TPU will make your filament collection even easier to organize. Spool Pull-Out Part In most cases, you can simply open the lid and remove the spool by hand. If the spool is difficult to reach, use the included filament pull-out part. Pulling this part forward makes it easier to bring the spool toward the front of the case. The rear section of the pull-out part also includes a compartment for silica gel or another desiccant. Check the Humidity Without Opening the Case A small hygrometer can be installed in the lid. This allows you to check the internal humidity at any time without opening the case. A TPU gasket is installed between the lid and the case body. Double-sided tape is also used around the clear window to help reduce air leakage and maintain a stable internal humidity. This case does not include an active heating or drying function. It is designed to store filament that has already been dried and to help protect it from moisture when used together with desiccant. Required Parts 3D-Printed Parts Case body Lid TPU gasket Spool pull-out part Lid-locking bolt Lid-locking nut Printing the lid-locking nut with the same filament stored inside the case allows it to be used as a color sample. Additional Parts Small Hygrometer ×1 A small rectangular hygrometer is recommended. Desiccant Silica gel or a similar desiccant can be used. Clear Sheet ×1 Acrylic, PVC, or another transparent sheet can be used. Size: 74 × 185 mm Thickness supported by the standard model: 0.5–0.6 mm The thickness of commonly available clear sheets may vary depending on your region or supplier. If you would like to use a different thickness, such as a 1 mm sheet, please leave a comment with the required thickness. Even if there is only one request, I plan to prepare a lid file that supports that thickness. M3 Socket Head Cap Screws ×2 Length: 25～30 mm These screws are used as hinge pins on the left and right sides of the lid. No nuts are used with these M4 screws. They are simply inserted from both sides. Double-Sided Tape Width: 5 mm This is used to attach the clear sheet and the hygrometer. Assembly Instructions 1. Install the Printed Lid-Locking Bolt Install the 3D-printed lid-locking bolt into the hook on the inside of the case body. Insert the part from inside the case, then slide it sideways along the hook until it is secured. Check the photos for the correct position and orientation. The part used in this step is the 3D-printed lid-locking bolt. It is not one of the metal M4 screws. 2. Install the TPU Gasket Fit the TPU gasket around the front opening of the case body. Make sure the gasket is installed evenly and is not twisted or lifted away from the surface. Any twisting or lifting may affect how well the lid seals against the case. 3. Attach the Clear Sheet to the Lid The rear side of the lid has a recessed area for attaching the clear sheet. Apply 5 mm-wide double-sided tape around this recessed area. The tape should form a continuous loop around the window without any gaps. Gaps may allow air to enter the case and reduce the effectiveness of the seal. Remove the protective backing from the tape and attach the clear sheet, cut to 74 × 185 mm. Align the clear sheet carefully. If the sheet is misaligned, it may interfere with the TPU gasket and reduce the effectiveness of the seal. Before permanently attaching it, confirm that the sheet fits correctly in the intended position. 4. Install the Hygrometer Attach the small hygrometer to the smaller window in the lid. Secure it directly with a small amount of double-sided tape. Use only the minimum amount of tape needed to hold the hygrometer in place. If it is attached too firmly, it may be difficult to remove when replacing the hygrometer or disposing of the case. 5. Attach the Lid to the Case Body Align the hinge sections on both sides of the lid with the holes in the case body. Insert one M4 socket head cap screw from each side. Do not tighten the M3 screws. Simply insert them from the left and right sides. No nuts are used in this step. Insert each screw only far enough that it does not significantly protrude from the side of the case. After installation, check that the lid opens and closes smoothly. 6. Insert the Spool Pull-Out Part If you are using desiccant, place it in the compartment at the rear of the filament pull-out part. Insert the pull-out part into the rear of the case body. Place the filament spool on top of it. 7. Install the Lid-Locking Nut Close the lid and attach the 3D-printed lid-locking nut from the front. Printing this nut with the same filament stored inside the case allows it to be used as a color sample for identifying the contents. You can also add a label showing the material type, such as PLA, PETG, ABS, or TPU. How to Use Remove the lid-locking nut and open the lid toward the front. Remove the filament spool directly by hand. If the spool is difficult to reach, pull the filament pull-out part toward the front of the case. Each case can be opened individually while the cases remain stacked vertically or arranged side by side. Important Notes This case is designed to store already-dried filament and help reduce moisture absorption during storage. It does not actively dry filament that has already absorbed a large amount of moisture. When necessary, dry the filament with a filament dryer before placing it in the case. The position of the clear sheet, gaps in the double-sided tape, and the condition of the TPU gasket will affect the quality of the seal. After assembly, check the following: The clear sheet is correctly aligned and is not lifting away from the lid. There are no gaps in the double-sided tape. The TPU gasket is not twisted or lifted. The lid opens and closes smoothly. The M3 screws do not significantly protrude from the sides of the case. The hygrometer is securely attached. Check the hygrometer regularly and replace or regenerate the desiccant when necessary.

description: A1 Vibration Damping Pods Inspired from the use of damping in the A2L. These mount to the brace that connects the X-axis to the Z-axis screws instead of the gantry. I don't have the equipment, nor interest to do a bunch of testing to say how effective these may be in this application on this device. Feel free to test and comment with your results below. * Assembly- Fill each compartment to approximately ¾ full. I used a hobby syringe. Make sure to fill them equally so they weigh the same on each side! Use a scale to weigh each compartment as you fill them. Mine weighed 57grams each, once filled. Your results may vary. but, if they weigh the same as mine we can be twinzies. Seal each compartment by gluing a plug in the fill port. Or fill each port with a glue plug. Insert into X-axis brace from the top. Will be a snug fit by design. Grunting and cursing may ease the process. Make sure they sit all the way down. My brackets had some significant burrs, so you may need to de-burr or perform some fitment of the Pods. Insert clip from below. Or lower the printer onto the clip. Secure bottom and pod together with the M3x6 button head coarse thread screw. Tighten until something snaps! This project intends to reduce the amount of harmful gases produced during the 3D printing process by creating a slight negative pressure in the chamber to reduce or eliminate them leaking out. It does this by automatically controlling a fume extractor fan based on what your Bambu printers are doing. It uses a 3D printed filter box with active charcoal and an ESP32 to poll one or two Bambu printers for status information and ramp a set of fans up and down based on the printer status. It also gives basic printer status information through a dashboard. Although this project was initially designed around two printers it can easily be used for one printer with no modifications other than printing a cap for the non-used intake. In fact I personally recommended using one printer per filter box for simplicity. Using more than two printers is also possible but is an advanced use case requiring some modifications to the code or possibly the 3D printed model and is not required for a standard one or two printer setup. This is a advanced build involving a printed filter box, a ESP32 micro controller, programming, wiring, and a read-only cloud connection between the ESP32 and your Bambu account. I tried to make it as simple as possible without requiring soldering, heat-sets, etc but it is still a involved project. I do not want to discourage anyone from attempting this but it does have multiple pieces that all need to come together for a successful working system. There are two print profiles with active carbon: One with a open bottom which makes it easier to mount the components but requires a longer print time due to supports and one with a solid bottom that prints quicker but might be a little harder to navigate inside. In my pictures I used the open bottom but the closed bottom is sturdier. You can also save some time by using a 0.6 nozzle @ 0.18 layer height or for the solid bottom model switching the “lid” color to match the box color. The lid for each version slides in so you have to be mindful of shrinkage. In my example, and in the print profiles, I'm using Bambu ABS for the box and Bambu ABS-GF for the lids as it has minimal shrinkage. The third print profile is for those of you that already vent to the outside but want to automate this process. It's a simple scaled down box with one input and one output and no filters but otherwise follows the same system and logic. The full read-me, Bill of Material, programming code, assembly instructions, and programming guide is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ADYDesigns/BambuAFE/ This project also relies on getting the fumes from your printer to this project. My recommendation is @Made.In.Meidling exhaust system: https://makerworld.com/en/models/1880330-slim-h2-quicklock-exhaust-system-updated . Instead of reinventing the wheel I used, with permission, the threaded connections from their system on my model so it is 100% compatible with theirs. NOTE : Bambu can, at any time, change the access to printer status through their cloud. If that does happen there is already code in place so you may manually turn on the fans using a single potentiometer. Test Supporti PLA vs Interfaccia PETG In questo test ho confrontato due configurazioni di supporto per verificare la qualità della superficie e la facilità di rimozione: Configurazione 1 (sinistra) Modello: PLA Supporti principali: PLA Interfaccia di contatto: PETG Configurazione 2 (destra) Modello: PLA Supporti e interfaccia: PLA Risultati La combinazione PLA + PETG ha mostrato una separazione quasi perfetta tra pezzo e supporto. Grazie alla scarsa adesione tra i due materiali, l'interfaccia in PETG si stacca facilmente lasciando una superficie più pulita e definita. Con i supporti realizzati interamente in PLA, invece, l'adesione è maggiore: la rimozione richiede più forza e la superficie inferiore tende a non presentare molti segni lasciati dai supporti grazie ai test effettuati e profilo calibrato (alla fine ti metterò il link per il profilo calibrato). Vantaggi dell'interfaccia PETG ✅ Supporti più facili da rimuovere ✅ Migliore finitura delle superfici supportate ✅ Minore rischio di danneggiare il pezzo durante la rimozione ✅ Possibilità di ridurre il gap dell'interfaccia per ottenere dettagli migliori Nota Importante La tecnica funziona in entrambe le direzioni: Pezzo in PLA + interfaccia supporti in PETG Pezzo in PETG + interfaccia supporti in PLA Poiché PLA e PETG aderiscono poco tra loro, è possibile utilizzare uno dei due materiali come interfaccia di separazione per ottenere supporti facilmente removibili. Impostazioni consigliate Materiale modello: PLA o PETG Materiale interfaccia supporti: materiale opposto al modello Interfaccia supporti: 2-4 layer Distanza Z superiore: 0 mm (o molto ridotta) Torre di spurgo consigliata per evitare contaminazioni tra i materiali Conclusione Se disponi di una stampante con AMS o doppio estrusore, utilizzare un materiale diverso per l'interfaccia dei supporti è uno dei modi più efficaci per ottenere superfici migliori e supporti che si rimuovono quasi senza sforzo. In questo test la combinazione PLA/PETG ha dimostrato chiaramente il vantaggio rispetto ai supporti tradizionali realizzati con un solo materiale. description: TIP: Make several insertions and removals of the half nuts in your hand before you do the actual installation, it will break-in the joint and makes it easier to install UPDATE 1: To ease the rear installation, I designed a slightly different platform for locking the half-nut in place, print profile and instructions are updated. UPDATE: I slightly modified the nut to make it a little tighter (only 0.02mm increase of the tooth width). The print profile has been updated. Due to the tighter profile inserting the half nut parrallel to the platform edge (step 9) might be more difficult. I advise to insert it to the leadscrew at a slight angle and then rotate to verify it does not go too much beyond the front face. Also, the rear nut will be really hard to clip… You may want to cut a bit of the protrusion (one side or the other whether you're left or right-handed (or both)), it could make it easier. If you really cannot clip them together (it took me almost 20 minutes just to do it this time!), you will certainly have to do it from the back removing the rear panel. To avoid this, I will try to come up with a tool (done, see update 1) to make it easier from the front. _____________________________________________________________ One of the issue experienced on Bambu H2 printers is the leadscrew nut failing. The nut (mainly the rear nut) starts to develop wear until it fails completely with stripped thread. It does not happen on all printers and those which failed have several 1,000hrs of print time except on some occasions when it failed sooner. Bambu support is reacting well in those cases, providing a full leadscrew kit to replace the failed nut(s) and leadscrews but the replacement takes several hours and a lot of disassembly/re-assembly and you may not afford this down time especially if the failed printer is part of a print farm. My rear nut currently has about 0.85mm of play with about 1,800hrs of use. It is still printing fine and bamboo provided me with a leadscrew kit but I figured I could design a quick fix that take less than 10min for each nut replacement with no removal. I have made several prototypes for the 2-part nut to make sure it can easily clip but still require some force so that when clipped it operates like a whole nut. The installation posts and installation platforms have also required some thorough testing to make sure that without any removal and references from a new leadscrew installation, the clocking of the nut to the sliding support is still exactly right. This can be done as an interim fix until Bambu ships the leadscrew kit replacement to you or you can decide it to be a permanent fix. Although I only printed a dozen of models since the replacement of the 3 leadscrew nuts, I’m fairly confident although I cannot guarantee the nut longevity, that they may hold a long time and given how easy and quick they can now be replaced, I know I will let them on my printer and see how it goes in the long run. The nuts are printed in ASA and the rest of the kit in PLA. The nut replacement requires absolutely no other removal than the nuts themselves and the rear nut can be installed from inside the printer not even requiring removal of the back panel. Instructions: Do not fear the long instructions, it's really easy to do Note: The following instructions have steps numbered, 1,2,3... The process is mainly the same for the fronts or the rear nut but when it is different, there will be a 1.a or 5.a to define the changes for the rear nut. Bring the 2 half nuts you’ve just printed together and clip them between your thumb and index finger (you may need both hands for that initial assembly). You will then feel the force required to do it but this first installation will break-in a bit the assembly so that it will require a little bit less force during actual installation. Use a flat head screwdriver to separate the 2 halves using one of the slots provided on either side. Install the 3 posts around each of the linear rod. The posts simply clip around the rods. The rear post has a deeper recess that goes on the top to wrap around the top sliding bearing. The front post ends have different geometry, the smaller diameter goes at the bottom. Clip them so that the post slot is facing the leadscrew (required to be able to install the installation platforms later). In the menu access the Z travel and lower the bed until it touches the posts. Start with 10mm and finish with several passes of 1mm until the bed touches the posts. You will hear a slight humming from your Z motor when contact occurs. Keep the printer ON during the whole process, the Z motor will then stay energized so that the leadscrews cannot rotate. Note: Do one nut after the other to guarantee perfect alignment, start with the fronts as they are easier to do Remove the 3 screws holding the nut to its slider. The screws are coated with red Loctite so you will need a fair amount of force initially to break the bond and although they will still be somewhat hard to turn, they will then unscrew more easily. Tip: break the bond and slighly unscrew all 3 screws before removing them. Please use good hex driver or hex bits, the space is limited and please do not damage the hex on the screws or you will be in big trouble, use GOOD TOOLS (I wouldn't use the bambu allen key!) Insert the removal/guide tube around the leadscrew, slide it up against the bottom of the nut and rotate slightly until the 3 fingers insert into the 3 tapped hole. Unscrew the nut until it’s out of the slider and remove the guide Rotate the original nut to the bottom of the leadscrew Insert the front installation platform between the rod and the leadscrew 8.a. ( For the rear nut ). You should really keep the rear post in place if you can but if you really need more room, slide it out gently and remove it then install the installation platform from the back of the leadscrew. It will be a little difficult to install it but I can assure you it fits :). Place it up then rotate it down from the back Place the top half-nut (the one with the 2 holes) behind the leadscrew and engage the thread. The goal is to install it parallel to the front of the platform, it should easily engage the leadscrew and it should not move more when you move it clockwise (or just a tiny bit). 9.a. ( For the rear nut ). The goal is to install it parallel to the reference groove on the platform and it should not move more when you move it clockwise (or just a tiny bit). Keep the half-nut you’ve just installed on the leadscrew thread by pushing it with your fingers so it does not disengage. 10.a ( For the rear nut ). Install the nut lock behind the nut. Bring the lock forward against the rear of the nut without moving it and then push on the lock to lock it on the platform With your fingers still holding on the half-nut use your other hand to present the second half-nut in one of the cavity (the nuts have a chamfered groove on one side and a chamfered protrusion on the other so that they will perfectly align) 11.a ( For the rear nut ). The first insertion should be on the left side which will make full insertion later easier Clip the 2 half-nuts together by pressing between your thumb and index finger (you will certainly also need your other hand for the force required to clip the 2 half-nuts). This force is per design but not that much that it can’t be easily done. If you feel it needs a lot of force, it might means you did not align them correctly. 12.a ( For the rear nut ). Push hard with your thumb against the open side to clip. The nut lock will keep the nut in position. Note: You can verify the nut is placed properly on the leadscrew by unscrewing and screwing it back down to the platform, it should stay parallel to the front of it (a minor angle is OK). Optionally, if your original nut is not stripped completely and you can still screw it on the leadscrew, you can double-check the alignment by removing the platform, bring both original and plastic nut together, and check the hole alignment by inserting a piece of filament in any one of the holes. If it’s not aligned, it means you have jumped one tooth during installation, remove the half-nut (a slot is provided on both sides to insert a flat head screwdriver) and re-do. Remove the platform and rotate the original nut all the way down if it’s not already there. Take a 1minute break to breeze until you proceed Insert the guide tool around the leadscrew and insert it in the 3 holes of the new nut. 15.a. ( For the rear nut ). Re-install by sliding back in the rear post you removed at step 9.a., rotate it to the side so that you have enough room to rotate the guide tool with one or 2 fingers :) While keeping the bed seated against the post by pushing down on the slider, rotate the tool up until the nut contacts the inner bottom of the slider. With the bed pushed down and the nut fully in contact, the holes should almost align. You should need to slightly unscrew just a little bit to make them align nicely. If it requires more than just a bit (about a hole size or just a hair more), you may have done the installation wrong and need to redo it. Insert the 3 new screws (BT3x10), though the slider and into the nuts and screw them on an alternating pattern until they are fully seated (seated only not tightened). Move up the bed in the menu 2 mm and seat the screws again on an alternating pattern (seated only not tightened). Now, unscrew them all one half turn so that the nut can slightly move around its position Move up the bed in the menu 10mm Remove the guide tube, the 3 posts and anything you may have placed below the bed In the menu bring the bed down until it contacts the bottom of the printer (same as before, several 10mm travels initially, then 1mm steps until contact) Now you can screw tight the 3 nut screws (the leadscrew have some degrees of liberty in all directions but not at the bottom where it is guided by the bearing, this is why the final tightening of the nut needs to be done there so that it’s fully concentric to the leadscrew). Do the same for the 2 other nuts. DONE! Note: When you’re done replacing the 3 nuts, run a bed levelling calibration. Note: I added for download a gcode file for breaking-in the freshly new installed nuts. Makerworld does not accept gcode as a file so I renamed it .stp to upload. Download it from the STL/CAD Files download option, rename the .stp to .gcode and put it at the root of your USB key, you can then print the gcode from the printer's menu. What the gcode does is a homing followed by 6 travels up and down of the bed. The file is the same for H2S/H2D/H2C. Note: You may notice that when all nuts are replaced and you bring the bed fully down against the bottom of the printer, all 3 sliders seat nicely with no gap on any of the 3 which is certainly better than when you received your printer (one of my slider had a couple of tenths gap). It means assembly is perfect but a tramming may be required if it was not the condition before replacement… When I replaced my nuts, I checked my tramming but as I only had a 0.1mm max bed out of tram from left to right and front to back, I left it like that and just run a bed levelling calibration. I left the tramming for later :). At least just do a quick tramming check at least. It shouldn't be too offset and that's a good check that the installation was done properly. Note: The removed nuts are now sitting at the bottom of the leadscrew, they will not reduce the vertical travel as they will just bury in the slider with the bed is fully at the bottom but I was afraid they could behave as a jam nut against the bearing and the leadscrew threads and risking locking the leadscrew. It did not happen to me yet certainly due to some slack in the worn nut threads that prevented it but your mileage may vary. You may want to put a safety wire or a cable tie or a piece of tape around the leadscrew below the nut for extra safety so it will not stay fully down against the bearing.

So funny story. I love printing things. Therefore I have a lot of plastic waste from poop to supports etc…. A while ago my husband says “your going to need a dumpster for all that plastic”. Then my neighbor noticed the several bags of plastic “poop” I have and said the exact thing. And only when my nephew comes over and says the same thing once again I thought to myself, I need to make a little dumpster to catch all the poop my printer makes. I pictured the Home Alone 2 movie where the house Kevin rigs up has a chute outside the window going into a dumpster. So that's where the idea for project came from. There are tons of “poop” bins and baskets for the other printers but I wanted to make one for my new Bambu Lab A2L printer. She's a beast. Very detailed and prints well. I love it. It does shake the house though being a large sized bed slinger. I have been printing on silent mode to calm it down in most cases. This took me a week to create. A little longer than usual but I needed to get the tolerances perfecta. My main goal was to make it easy and reliable to print. That was the challenge. I tried several ways to get the chute to print as one piece but it never worked out. So clip or bracket that connects to the printer is separate and has to be glued to the chute. I did make a connection socket so the two fit together perfectly so all is needed is a drop of cyanoacrylate glue (Super Glue) or something similar on each edge of the connection opening and hold it in place for the appropriate time (depending on your glue). I have printed 19 sets of the chute and bracket and glued them together successfully with no problem. Supports were absolutely necessary to accomplish my goal. I tried to keep the settings simple but tweaked the settings like the top and bottom Z distance, speed etc… to get dumpster and chute to come out clean. Just be sure to keep my settings. You can add to them if you please but it wont be necessary as you can tell by my photos. I have had several people that don't have a printer me to print them one just because they wanted the cute little bin. I have even been changing the sizes per their requests. The dumpster itself is scalable and you can make a smaller or larger one depending on your needs. I am sure it will have many uses. Schwingungskompensation für A1 und A2L Bambu Lab hat mit dem A2L gezeigt, wie wirkungsvoll eine adaptive Schwingungskompensation das Druckbild verbessern kann. Das zugrunde liegende Prinzip ist ebenso einfach wie bewährt und findet auch in hochwertigen Werkzeugen Anwendung. Ein rückstoßfreier Hammer etwa besitzt eine Kammer, die mit Stahlschrot oder Sand gefüllt ist. Beim Aufprall bewegt sich das Füllmaterial zeitversetzt nach, absorbiert einen Teil der Rückprallenergie und reduziert so unerwünschte Schwingungen. Das Ergebnis ist eine kontrolliertere Bewegung ohne störendes Hüpfen oder Nachfedern. Da der Querträger des A2L dieselben Abmessungen aufweist, liegt es nahe, dieses Dämpferkonzept auch dort einzusetzen. Gerade bei hohen Druckgeschwindigkeiten lässt sich das Schwingungsverhalten dadurch zusätzlich optimieren. Aus diesem Grund habe ich für den A1 und A2L einen Schwingungsdämpfer entwickelt. Er absorbiert Bewegungsenergie sowohl in der X- als auch in der Y-Achse und trägt damit zu einem ruhigeren Lauf des Druckers bei. Besonders dann, wenn das AMS lite oder Filament-Rollen oben auf dem Gerät montiert sind, werden störende Bewegungen deutlich reduziert. Das sorgt insbesondere bei schnellen Druckvorgängen für ein saubereres und gleichmäßigeres Druckbild. Die Schwingungskompensatoren bestehen aus einem Behälter mit integrierten Schwallwänden. Diese begrenzen die freie Bewegung des Füllmaterials, erhöhen die Reibung im Inneren und verbessern dadurch die Energieabsorption. Ihre volle Wirkung entfalten die Dämpfer vor allem bei kleinen, schnellen Bewegungen. Material Für die Montage werden weder Klebstoff noch Schrauben benötigt. Zum Befüllen empfehle ich feinkörnigen Sand, da er eine besonders gute Dämpfungswirkung ermöglicht. Druck Für den Druck eignet sich PETG besonders gut, da die Halteklammern über den oberen Träger gesteckt werden und PLA dafür in der Regel zu spröde ist. Montage Befüllen Sie die Behälter bis zur Oberkante der Schwallwände mit Sand. Nach oben sollte etwas Luft verbleiben, damit sich das Füllmaterial frei bewegen kann. Verschließen Sie die Behälter mit den Deckeln und stecken Sie anschließend die seitlichen Clips mit der Öffnung nach unten auf. Die Form des Deckels gibt die korrekte Position automatisch vor. Stecken Sie die Schwingungsdämpfer links und rechts auf den oberen Querträger des Druckers auf. Die Dämpfer sind zudem kompatibel, wenn das AMS lite oben montiert ist. Funktionsprüfung Nach dem Druck können Sie die Wirkung der Dämpfer direkt prüfen: Füllen Sie eine Kammer wie beschrieben mit Sand, verschließen Sie beide Kammern mit den Deckeln und fixieren Sie sie mit den Clips. Schütteln Sie anschließend zunächst den leeren und danach den gefüllten Absorber mit der Hand. Der Unterschied in der Dämpfungswirkung ist dabei deutlich spürbar. Wichtig Vergessen Sie nicht nach der Montage eine neue Kalibrierung des Druckers durchzuführen!

CUSTOMIZABLE DIY FILAMENT/BOOK SHELF SEVERAL RISER OPTIONS CUSTOMIZE TO FIT YOUR SPACE NOTE: REQUIRES SOME WORK WITH WOOD As part of my new print room, I designed this DIY shelf system to maximize the space I had available for my filament storage dry boxes and keep them organized. At the same time l wanted something truly unique and nice to look at. I decided to share it here in case others want to try it themselves. Please read all of the information and the attached instructions before starting. Overall, it may not be a huge cost savings compared to an Ikea or other purchasable bookshelf (though the larger it is the more it will save), but being able to make it the exact length and height you want is not possible with those options. Plus, the looks of this are so much better IMO. The riser options include: Diamondplate Pattern Lattice Pattern Square & Compass Vertical Bolts (these are only recommended for middle risers) FYI If you are interested in the filament labels or drybox kits shown in the pictures, you can find them here: https://makerworld.com/en/models/1193463-filament-labels-with-logos https://makerworld.com/en/models/2561229-4l-dry-box-kit-for-outer-spool-desiccant-trays ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ PURCHASED PARTS SHELVES The shelves themselves are made of ¾” wood and the risers are designed to fit a shelf depth of 234mm (9-3/8”). Your shelf length will be whatever length you want for your needs (more on that in the instructions below). This means you can source the shelving a number of different ways. Buy standard ¾” shelf boards and trim them to size. The ends are covered and the back not visible so you could get them pre-finished if you can make clean cuts. Buy a ¾” MDF sheet and cut or have the hardware store cut to the correct depth and whatever length you decide, then paint as needed. This is the option I chose. Buy a ¾” plywood sheet and cut or have the hardware store cut to the correct depth and whatever length you decide. Then you would need to add edging to the front edge to cover the layer lines before painting. HARDWARE Threaded wood inserts – ¼” or M6 x ¾” or 20mm (9) Inserts are required PER SHELF I used these: https://a.co/d/0hchaaFy Flattened or Button Head Screws – ¼”x1-1/2” or M6x35 (18) screws per intermediate shelf, (9) screws per top and bottom shelf I used these: https://a.co/d/00rvAgmG IF you are going to use the Square and Compass Risers, you will also need (4) M5 heat press inserts (any length up to 12mm max) and (4) M5x20mm Socket Head Screws PER RISER to connect the pieces together. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- PRINTED PARTS You will need the following printed parts from the print profile of your choice: RISERS – Selection and quantity are up to you. Generally, you will need 2 risers per shelf and if you feel it needs a middle riser. Bolt Risers are only recommended as a middle riser and require 3 per riser. Square and Compass Risers include 3 pieces per riser that need assembled – main riser, top, and bottom. RISER CONNECTORS – These slide onto the shelf and connect to the risers. You will need 2 side connectors (and 1 middle connector if you chose a middle riser) per shelf. The top shelf has special Top Riser Connectors. Bolt Risers do not need any Riser Connectors but are only recommended as a middle riser. BOLT SPACERS – These get bolted to the shelves to interconnect the risers and riser connectors. You will need the same quantity as the screws – 18 per intermediate shelf, 9 per top and bottom shelf. FEET - You can attach any feet of your liking to the bottom using the ¼" threaded holes. The ones in the picture which I recommend I had previously released here: https://makerworld.com/en/models/2498728-hd-adjustable-leveling-foot Now let’s talk about print orientation. There are 2 print profiles – one with the risers and connectors oriented flat on the bed, and one with risers and connectors oriented vertically. Depending on your filament of choice, printing orientation will change how the color looks. Square & Compass Risers and Bolt Risers must be printed vertically unless you are willing to get creative with supports. Vertical printing creates a higher resolution but is much more challenging to print. The hardest part with vertical printing is the Riser Connectors because the opening for the shelf requires supports. You can use a special support material but this adds layer time which can cause a “benchy hull” line from the big difference in layer time. Not using special support material (like I didn’t) creates a rough interface. Not too big of a deal since it is sitting flat against the shelf, but I had to make little trim pieces to cover the exposed outer edge. Those are included if you need them. If you like the look or the filament color doesn't change, another option would be to print the risers vertically and the connectors flat. This would be kind of the “best of both worlds”. I chose a shiny filament, so orientation made a big difference in the color. Here is a comparison of the two print orientations: ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- FILAMENT SELECTION The majority of the loading is in compression (buckling) so material requirements aren’t too bad. I recommend a MINIMUM of a PLA+ that has decent impact strength. A good Tough PLA+ like the one Bambu has, Sunlu’s PLA+ 2.0, or Polymaker Polylite PLA PRO would be decent options. I would avoid basic matte or silk PLA’s as their brittleness and layer adhesion may not make it appropriate. PETG will generally hold up a little better but is more difficult to print. I chose Tinmorry Space Grey Metallic PETG because it gave me a nice “steel” look and I printed vertically. Seams and retraction were a big challenge however and took me a couple tries. I have attached the assembly instruction and basic assembly dimensions. Length is based on the one I built and fit the dry boxes shown in the pictures perfectly, but you can adjust to the length you want for your needs. model_name: 一板测全机｜打印机综合测试+填充结构示意（mini可打）
tags: 测试|mini|综合测试|填充|结构示意
description: 一板在手，测试无忧！ 这是一个集成了多种经典校准项目的3D打印综合测试模型，无需打印多个测试件，即可快速评估打印机的整体状态与参数设置。 模型尺寸小巧，耗材消耗少，适合： ✓ 新打印机验机 ✓ 更换耗材后校准 ✓ 调整切片参数验证 ✓ 打印机维护保养检查 ✓ 不同材料打印性能对比 测试项目说明 1. 收缩率测试（Shrinkage） 用于检测模型实际尺寸与设计尺寸的偏差。 重点观察： 长度尺寸是否准确 XY方向收缩情况 常见问题： 尺寸偏小 孔位缩小 装配件配合困难 可能原因： 材料收缩率较大 流量设置过高 冷却不足 解决方案： 调整XY补偿 校准Flow Ratio 优化打印温度 2. 悬垂测试（Overhang） 用于评估无需支撑时的打印能力。 测试角度： 10°~80° 重点观察： 边缘下垂 表面粗糙 层线变形 塌腰等 可能原因： 风扇风量不足 打印温度过高 打印速度过快 角度过大，超过打印极限 解决方案： 增大冷却风量 降低喷嘴温度 减小外壁速度 添加支撑 3. 搭桥测试（Bridging） 用于测试跨空打印能力。 重点观察： 中间是否下垂 是否出现拉丝 桥面是否平整 可能原因： 冷却不足 挤出量过小 速度设置不合理 解决方案： 提高桥接风扇速度 加大桥接流量 4. 球形效果测试（Sphere Quality） 用于检测曲面打印质量。 重点观察： 圆滑程度 层纹均匀性 接缝表现 可能原因： Z轴抖动 振纹（Ghosting） 机械间隙 解决方案： 检查皮带张力 校准Z轴 5. 拉丝测试（Stringing） 通过多个尖塔检测耗材拉丝情况。 重点观察： 塔之间是否出现细丝 丝线粗细程度 可能原因： 回抽不足 温度过高 耗材受潮 解决方案： 增大回抽距离 降低打印温度 烘干耗材 6. 尖锥测试（Spike Test） 用于测试尖端细节表现能力。 重点观察： 尖端是否完整 是否融化变钝 可能原因： 温度过高 冷却不足 解决方案： 降低温度 提高最小层时间 增加冷却风量 7. 色卡测试（Color Sample） 方便记录不同厚度耗材颜色效果。 用途： 耗材展示 配色参考 打印样品留档 8. 薄壁测试（Thin Wall） 测试打印机极限壁厚能力。 重点观察： 是否缺层 是否断裂 实际壁厚误差 可能原因： 流量不准 喷嘴磨损 挤出系统异常 解决方案： 校准流量 检查喷嘴状态 9. 表面质量测试（Surface Finish） 观察打印层纹与整体表面表现。 重点观察： 层纹均匀性 振纹 接缝质量 可能原因： 速度过快 机械共振 温度不匹配 解决方案： 调整加速度 优化打印温度 校准流量 10. 填充结构展示（Infill Pattern） 模型内置拓竹切片软件的全部填充结构： 可用于： 学习不同填充结构特点 对比强度与打印速度 如果这个模型对你有所帮助，欢迎点赞、助力、收藏并上传你的打印成果！ 祝大家打印顺利，层层完美！

description: AMS HT Side Mount für Bambu Lab H2 Serie Diese Halterung ermöglicht es, das AMS HT seitlich am oberen Rahmen eines Druckers der H2-Serie zu befestigen. Dadurch kann TPU direkt über die Bypass-Öffnung des AMS HT zum Druckkopf geführt werden. Der große Vorteil dieser Positionierung ist der extrem kurze und nahezu geradlinige Filamentweg. Das reduziert den Wiederstand beim fördern des Filaments auf ein Minimum und verbessert insbesondere den Druck mit sehr weichen TPU-Filamenten, die empfindlich auf lange oder stark gekrümmte Filamentwege reagieren. Zusätzlich kann das AMS HT während des Drucks weiterhin als Filamenttrockner genutzt werden. So bleibt das TPU während des gesamten Druckvorgangs trocken, was die Druckqualität zusätzlich verbessert. Einfache Konstruktion Die Halterung besteht aus drei Steckteilen, die ohne Schrauben oder weiteres Montagematerial zusammengesteckt werden. Diese Bauweise bietet mehrere Vorteile: Sehr einfacher und zuverlässiger Druck. Nur eines der drei Bauteile benötigt eine winzige Stützstruktur. Die Halterung lässt sich jederzeit wieder zerlegen und dadurch besonders platzsparend verstauen. Hinweis: Je nach verwendeten Material und Kalibrierung des Druckers und Filament, kann es sein, dass die Steckverbindung schwergängig ist. Versuche nicht die Teile mit Gewalt zusammen zu stecken! In diesen Fall ist es hilfreich die Steckverbinder mit etwas Schlafpapier nach zu arbeiten. Etwas Gleitmittel wie Balistol oder WD40 kann ebenfalls helfen. Einfache Montage Für die Montage muss lediglich der Glasdeckel des Druckers entfernt werden. Anschließend wird die Halterung einfach über den oberen Rand des Druckers gesteckt. Das AMS HT wird danach nur auf der Halterung abgestellt - ganz ohne zusätzliche Befestigung. If there is no exhaust port on the back panel, then you have an early version of the printer and will need to order the External Exhaust Fan Kit + Rear Panel option from Bambu (which doesn't cost extra). And install the new rear panel before you can install the External Exhaust Fan upgrade. Instructions installing the rear panel are here . NOTE: 5 output stage options are currently offered, distributed across several print profiles: Low Profile Vertical Active Fan Vent P2S X2D Vx.3m, Plate 4 - 3.75 inch hose adapter Low Profile Active P2S Fan Vent Vx.3mf, Plate 3 - Fan Grille Low Profile Fan Vent P2S 75mm Hose Adapter Vx.3MF, Plate 1 - 75mm hose adapter Low Profile Fan Vent P2S X2D Rt Angle Hose Adapters Vx.3MF, Plate 1 or 3 - 3.75 inch adapter Low Profile Fan Vent P2S X2D Rt Angle Hose Adapters Vx.3MF, Plate 2 or 4 - 75mm adapter This model is divided into 4 parts: the Base Module, Vertical Extension, Fan Module, and Output Stage (Hose Adapter/Fan Grille). This partitioning allows easy modification of any component without needing to reprint the other components. For example, the Hose Adapter can be easily replaced to support different hose sizes. Let me know in the comments the Inner Diameter (ID) of the particular hose that you need. Assembly Base Assembly The first step is to assemble the Fan Vent Base. The two types of clips (as shown in Figure 1 ) are inserted into the Fan Vent Base (Low Profile Fan Vent P2S V4.stl) in the positions indicated in Figure 2 . Figure 1 : Low Profile Fan Vent Clips Be sure to orientate all the clips to point in the same direction, as indicated by the green arrow in Figure 2 . Then insert the BT2x5 self-tapping screws, provided with the Bambu kit, from the opposite side (see the green arrows in Figure 15 ) and secure the Clips with the screws. Figure 2 : Base Clip Attachment Finally apply the pre-cut black Foam Tape provided with the Bambu Kit to the Base. Confirm the correct position before pasting to avoid errors. Ensure the foam is aligned with the edge, and paste the four strips of top foam one by one as shown in Figure 2 . If you have an X2D and can't peel the tape of the factory fan cover, search for "1mm foam tape" on Amazon, they offer many options. If available, insert the External Exhaust Air Filter . Fan Module The next step is to assemble the Fan Module. Latches Each Latch consists of two parts: Body and Latch. First install the Latch Body part ( Figure 3 ) on the fan Module connector, then insert two BT2x5 self-tapping screws as indicated by the green arrows and tighten them on the both sides to attach it to the Latch Body. Note: The screws act as shafts. Do not over-tighten them otherwise the Latch will not work smoothly. Figure 3 : Latch Body Installation Next install the Latch Latch part ( Figure 4 ) on the fan Module connector, then insert two BT2x5 self-tapping screws as indicated by the green arrows and tighten them on the both sides to attach it to the Latch Body. Figure 4 : Latch Latch Installation Now use the same process to attach the Latch components on the opposite of the Fan Module for the Base, and on the top and bottom of the Fan Module for the Hose Adapter, as shown in Figure 5 . Figure 5 : Hose Adapter Latches Fan Installation Before continuing remove any leftover support material from around the inside of the Connector Holes ( Figure 6 ) and the ‘top’ inside surface of the PCB case (as indicated by the blue arrow in Figure 6 ). And ensure that PCB connectors fit through the holes, and the PCB fits snugly against the top surface of the PCB case. Route the fan cable through the Fan Cable Hole as shown in Figure 6 and Figure 8 . Figure 6 : PCB Case Then press the fan into the Fan Module with the orientation shown in Figure 7 , while pulling on the fan cable. Note that the gasket that wraps around the fan is facing out. Also the airflow direction arrow on the side of the fan must be facing out as well. The surface of the fan should be flush with the surface of the fan module. Figure 7 : Fan Orientation PCB Installation Connect the Fan Cable to the PCB then fit the connectors into the connector holes ( Figure 6 ) and rotate the PCB so that it flat against the bottom of the PCB case. description: Spulenadapter für 250 Gramm Spulen mit einfacher Anpassung je nach Spulenbreite oder Innenduchmesser / Kerndurchmesser der Spule!! Adapter sollte für nahezu jede Spule passen, er kann sehr einfach angepasst werden ohne CAD!! Siehe untenstehende Beschreibungen…! Druckprofile Standard: “Spulenadapter ASA” und "Spulenadapter PETG": Da ich keinen passenden Spulenadapter für meine 250 Gramm Spulen gefunden haben (250 Gramm Spulen von 3D Jake (PLA) und Spulen von RECREUS (TPU Spulen: zum Trocknen im AMS HT)), habe ich diesen hier konstruiert. Dieser passen für meine 250 Gramm-Spulen von 3D JAKE und von RECREUS welche einen Innenduchmesser (Spulenkern) von ca. 52 mm bis 53 mm haben, ca. 42 mm bis 43 mm breit sind und einen Aussendurchmesser von 139 mm bis 142 mm. Der Spulenadapter passt für mein AMS 2 PRO und auch für mein AMS HT und da ich den Adapter auch für das AMS HT verwende habe ich eine Variante aus PETG und auch eine Variante aus ASA gedruckt. Die Druckprofile sind mit Modifier ausgeführt wodurch nur der Bereich mit dem Gewinde eine höhere Wandanzahl aufweist wodurch beim Drucken Filament gespart wird aber die Spule trotzdem sehr stabil ist. Das Aussengewinde des Körper 1 ist 40 mm lang und versinkt im Körper 2 ca. 16 mm weit, im zusammengeschraubtem Zustand hat die Spule dann eine Breite von ca. 67 mm mit meinen oben genannten Spulen. Druckprofil: “Körper 2 mit durchgängigem Gewinde” Bei diesem Druckprofil ist das Gewinde des Körper 2 durchgehen wodurch das Aussengewinde des Körper 1 durch den Körper 2 hindurch geschraubt werden kann damit der Spulenadapter auch für Spulen mit einer anderen Spulenbreite oder Innendurchmesser / Kerndurchmesser passt. Bitte hier darauf achten, dass das überstehende Gewinde, bei sehr schmalen Spulen, nicht im AMS ansteht oder schleift!! Druckprofil: "Körper1 Gewindelänge anpassbar" Anpassen des Körper 1 für Spulen mit anderer Spulenbreiten oder anderem Innendurchmessern / Kernduchmessern: Da meine Konstruktion ein relativ langes Gewinde hat, im vergleich zu anderen Konstruktionen, kann man die Länge der Gewindes sehr einfach anpassen damit der Spulenadapter auch für Spulen mit einer anderen Spulenbreite oder einem anderen Innendurchmesser/Kerndurchmesser passt. Hierfür habe ich das Druckprofil “ Spulenadapter Gewindelänge 33 mm" hinzugefügt. Dieses beinhaltet eine “negatives Teil” durch welches die Länge des Gewindes, des Körper 1, auf 33 mm gekürzt wird. Wenn man diese 3mf im Slicer öffnet kann die Z - Position des "negative Teil", mit der Funktion “Bewegen”, sehr einfach geändert werden wodurch das Gewinde länger und kürzer gemacht werden kann und somit auch für andere 250 Gramm spulen angepasst werden kann. Einfach im Slicer das “negative Teil” anklicken , dann oben, in der Auswahlleiste, auf “Bewegen” klicken , und dann das “negative Teil” mit dem Blauen Pfeil nach oben oder nach unten schieben ODER in der Zeile “Position” in der Spalze “Z” den aktuellen Wert von 73 mm um die entsprechenden mm erhöhen oder reduzieren . Wenn man den Wert von 73 mm auf 70 mm reduziert wird die Gewindelänge von 33 mm auf 30 mm reduziert und passt somit für schmalere Spulen oder Spulen mit einem größeren Innendurchmesser. Somit kann man die Spule sehr einfach auf seine eigen Spulen angepasst werden. Ich wünsche viel Spaß beim Drucken und hoffe, dass dieser Druck auch für andere Personen so hilfreich ist wie dieser für mich ist.

description: Designed specifically for Cardboard Spools and built around one goal: maximum moisture exchange with zero compromises. Designed as part of an evolving system for filament storage and moisture control. This collection includes both print ready and fully parametric models, built to fit virtually every filament spool on the market. From common brands to odd dimensions, the goal is simple: one ecosystem that adapts instead of forcing compromises. Each desiccant holder is conceived, printed, and tested in real day to day use, not just tuned for screenshots. Airflow, capacity, refill handling, AMS compatibility, and long term durability are explored across multiple iterations. Spool Desiccant Collection: Spool Drying ⧸ Dry Filament Follow me If dry filament matters to you. A like or a boost directly supports further testing and new designs driven by daily use, not trends. Verified compatibility currently includes Cardboard spools from Bambu Lab, ERYONE, eSUN, GratKit, JAYO, Overture and Polymaker. PETG, ABS, ASA, PC or simple PLA, everything tested. No brims, no rafts, no support, no mouse ears, no experiments. The magic is in the geometry, not slicer tweaks. Pro Tip: Silent Silica, No Dust For an even quieter spool, place a small piece of melamine foam, roughly container opening shaped (1cm height), between the silica gel and the lid before closing it. The foam gently compresses the silica bed, preventing the beads from shifting while the spool rotates. This almost completely eliminates rattling and also minimizes abrasion, reducing long term silica dust. I've been using this simple trick for years, and it works remarkably well. FDM first geometry The slicer should not have to rescue the model. The model should already know how it wants to be printed. This model is not just shaped for printing. It is calculated for printing. Wall stacks, ring spacing, bridge positions, layer height, extrusion width, and remaining height compensation are all considered directly in the procedural geometry. Instead of leaving awkward half layer transitions and geometric leftovers for the slicer to improvise around, the model distributes and aligns critical structures around real FDM behavior. That means cleaner layers, fewer random toolpath decisions, less gap fill, more predictable bridging, and more consistent mechanical performance. In practice, this means you can throw the model into almost any slicer, enable the Arachne wall generator, set a 0.2 mm layer height, keep a standard 0.4 mm nozzle, and press slice. Printer choice matters surprisingly little because the geometry itself already guides the slicer toward clean and reliable extrusion paths. Model History 2026/06/22 Initial release

## Device Description Circle Bambu Monitor is a compact desktop display for monitoring Bambu Lab 3D printer status in real time. It is built around an ESP32-C3 SuperMini development board and a 1.28 inch round TFT display with a GC9A01 driver . The electronics are housed in a snap-fit 3D printed enclosure designed for a clean front view and easy rear access. The device connects to Wi-Fi and reads printer data from Home Assistant entities. It does not connect directly to the printer. Instead, it uses Home Assistant as the data source, which makes it flexible and easy to adapt to different Bambu Lab printer setups. ## Main Components - TENSTAR ESP32-C3 SuperMini development board - 1.28 inch round 240x240 TFT LCD display - GC9A01 display driver - 7-wire for display connection - 3D printed main body - 3D printed rear cover - USB-C power supply - Home Assistant with Bambu Lab integrations ## What It Does Circle Bambu Monitor shows the current status of a Bambu Lab printer on a small round display. It can display print progress, printer state, current print phase, temperatures, filament information, layer progress, print weight, estimated finish time, and a clock when the printer is idle. The device also includes a built-in web configuration interface. On first startup it creates its own Wi-Fi setup network. After connecting to it, the user can configure Wi-Fi, Home Assistant URL, access token, timezone, and the Home Assistant entities used for printer data. Firmware updates can be installed through the browser using the web installer, so users do not need to use the Arduino IDE. ## Data Source The device uses Home Assistant as its data source. It reads configured Home Assistant entities for: - Print phase - Print status - Print progress - Active filament slot - Estimated finish time - Nozzle temperature - Bed temperature - Current layer - Total layers - Filament weight ## Installation and Setup Guide Connect the display to the ESP32-C3 using the wiring diagram from the project documentation . The display uses SPI communication. Make sure all wires are connected correctly before powering the device. Open the web installer in a supported browser, such as Chrome or Edge. 1. Connect the ESP32-C3 to your computer using USB-C. 2. Click `Connect`. 3. Select the ESP32-C3 serial device. 4. Click `Install`. 5. Wait until flashing is complete. 6. Disconnect and reconnect the device if needed. After flashing, power on the device. If the device is not configured yet, it will start in setup mode and create its own Wi-Fi network. The display will show: - Wi-Fi network name - Setup password - Setup IP address Connect your phone or computer to the setup Wi-Fi network shown on the display. Then open the displayed IP address in your browser. In the web configuration page, enter: - Your Wi-Fi network - Wi-Fi password - Home Assistant URL (example http://192.168.1.100:8123) - Long-lived Home Assistant token After saving, the device will restart and connect to your Wi-Fi network. After restart, the device will no longer use the setup Wi-Fi network. Find the new IP address in your router, DHCP client list, or network device list. Open the device IP address in your browser to continue configuration. After the device connects to Home Assistant, the configuration page allows you to select the required entities. Configure entities for: - Print phase - Print status - Print progress - Active filament slot - Estimated finish time - Nozzle temperature - Bed temperature - Current layer - Total layers - Filament weight You can use the searchable entity fields to find matching Home Assistant entities. For example, typing “nozzle”, will show matching nozzle temperature entities. Entity names depend on your Home Assistant setup and integration. Configure Timezone - Select your timezone in the configuration page. This is used for Idle clock screen and estimated finish time display. Choose the timezone that matches your location.

model_name: BambuPlot Free Pen Plotter G-code Generator
description: Turn your Bambu Lab 3D printer into a pen plotter completely free, no subscriptions, no accounts, no uploads. Everything runs locally in your browser. The included test file uses the boat drawing shown in the preview image a detailed line-art illustration that works great as a first plot to verify your setup. When using the tool please consider using the included print profile test model. This helps me out and helps supporting this project with since i could not upload the Bambuplot file directly on Makerworld. ⚠ Read this first this is a tinkerer's project This tool is made for people who enjoy experimenting, troubleshooting, and figuring things out. It is not a plug-and-play product. It will probably not work perfectly on the first try , and that is completely normal. Getting a pen plotter working on a 3D printer requires patience: dialing in the Z height, finding the right pen, getting the paper flat, tuning the feed rates, and sometimes just accepting that the first few attempts are learning runs. I do not cover any damages to your printer, pen holder, bed, or any other part of your setup. Using this tool is entirely at your own risk. Sending custom G-code to a 3D printer always carries a risk of unexpected movement, crashes, or damage if settings are wrong. Always supervise the printer, always do a dry run first with the Z height raised so the pen cannot touch anything, and never leave it running unattended especially not on a first test. If you are not comfortable with that, this project is probably not for you yet but if you enjoy the process of making something work from scratch, welcome aboard. What is BambuPlot? BambuPlot is a single HTML file you download and open in your browser. It lets you design drawings and convert them into G-code that your Bambu Lab printer can execute with a pen instead of a nozzle. No internet connection is required after download — it runs 100% on your computer. Supported printers all current Bambu Lab models: Printer Bed size Notes A1 mini 180 × 180 mm A1 256 × 256 mm ✅ Tested P1P 256 × 256 mm P1S 256 × 256 mm P2S 256 × 256 mm X1 carbon 256 × 256 mm X2D 256 × 256 mm ✅ Tested A2L 330 × 320 mm H2D 325 × 320 mm H2S 340 × 320 mm A custom bed size option is also available for any other setup. What you can draw: Text three modes: single-stroke plotter font (looks like real handwriting), your own custom handwriting (draw each letter yourself, up to 5 versions per letter for variety so repeating letters never look identical), or filled outline using any of 13 fonts Shapes square, circle, triangle, star, line, with optional hatch fill Freehand draw directly on the bed preview with your mouse or stylus Images drop any photo or logo, adjust the threshold and line density, and convert it to plotted lines 3MF import drop a Bambu Lab .3mf file and BambuPlot extracts the 3D geometry and renders the top-down footprint as plottable paths, in either vector outline or hatch-fill mode What you need A Bambu Lab printer or anything else that takes gcode A pen holder that mounts on your toolhead (search MakerWorld or Printables for your specific model many free designs exist) A ballpoint pen that fits your holder Paper to draw on, attached to the bed (see bed preparation below) A way to get pure gcode on your printer (USB stick/microsd) Bed preparation protecting your print surface This is important. The pen tip will press directly down onto whatever is on your bed. Printing on bare paper placed directly on a softer printing bed can cause damage, especially with a stiff pen or too much Z pressure. My recommendation: place an old flat PEI sheet (Like mine from my old ender 3 v2), a thin sheet of plastic such as a folder cover or binder sheet, or any similarly flat, smooth piece of thin plastic underneath the paper. This gives the paper a firm, even surface to rest on and takes any wear from the pen instead of your actual print bed. An old or scratched PEI sheet you no longer use for printing is perfect for this. Attaching the paper: I use small magnets placed along the edges to hold the paper flat and in position they are quick to place, leave no residue, and hold very reliably. Other options that work fine include masking tape or binder clips on the edges. Whatever you use, make sure the paper is completely flat with no bubbles or lifted corners, as any unevenness will cause the pen pressure to vary across the drawing. How to download and open BambuPlot Go to : https://joep648.github.io/BambuPlot/bambuplot-v1.0.1.html to use it online. or Download the bambuplot.html file from: https://github.com/Joep648/BambuPlot/tree/main Open it with any modern browser (Firefox recommended for best performance Chrome and Edge work fine too, but Firefox handles large designs more smoothly) That is it no installation, no internet needed after that Step-by-step: from design to plot Step 1 Select your printer In the top bar, choose your printer model from the dropdown. The bed preview updates to the correct size. This ensures your G-code coordinates match your actual print surface. Step 2 Add content to the bed Use the tabs on the left panel: Text tab type your text, choose a style (single-stroke is best for plotting), adjust letter spacing and line spacing, then click Add text to bed Shapes tab pick a shape and click Add shape to bed . Enable Filled to get hatch-fill lines inside the shape Image tab click the drop zone or drag an image in. Adjust the threshold slider until the preview looks like clean black lines on white, then click Convert & add to bed . High-contrast line art like the included boat image gives the best results 3MF tab drag a .3mf file onto the drop zone. Choose Vector outline for a clean single-stroke contour of the model, or Top-down silhouette for a hatch-filled footprint Freehand in the Shapes tab, click Draw directly on bed and sketch with your mouse Step 3 Position and size your content Once an item appears on the bed preview: Drag the body of the item to move it Drag a corner handle to scale it the line density automatically recalculates to stay consistent at the new size Drag the white circle above the item to rotate it Use the Layers tab to show/hide, duplicate, or delete items Step 4 Configure pen settings Go to the Pen tab and set: Setting What it does Suggested starting value Z draw How far down the pen tip presses 0.5 mm Z lift How high the pen lifts between strokes 8 mm Draw feed Speed while drawing 1500 mm/min Travel feed Speed while moving between strokes 6000 mm/min Z move feed Speed of Z moves 600 mm/min Pen settle time Dwell after each Z move to prevent stray marks 120 ms These values are starting points every pen holder and pen combination is different. Adjust Z draw until the pen just barely touches the paper with light pressure. Step 5 Generate and download the G-code Click Generate G-code in the right panel. The code appears in the preview (large designs only show the first few thousand lines the full file is always in the download). Click the ⭳ button to download the .gcode file. Step 6 Send to the printer and plot My personal workflow: Home the printer manually via the touchscreen or Bambu Studio After homing, clip the pen holder onto the toolhead with the pen inserted Place your protective plastic sheet on the bed, lay the paper on top, and secure it with magnets, tape, or clips Start the file with in bambuplot Home all axes (G28) at start option turned off Always do a dry run first: temporarily raise the Z draw value by 5–10 mm so the pen stays off the paper, and watch the full motion to confirm the design lands in the right place before doing a real plot Alternative workflow using the dwell option: The Dwell after homing checkbox in the Pen tab inserts a G4 S30 command (a timed pause) after the G28 home command, giving you time to clip the pen on before plotting starts. This feature is experimental and untested I have not personally used it this way. Bambu printers do not support the standard M0 unconditional pause command, so a timed dwell is used as a workaround. If you try it, set the duration long enough to comfortably attach the pen holder (60 seconds or more). Tips for best results Use the right paper smooth, slightly heavier paper works best. Thin paper can wrinkle from pen pressure Ballpoint pens are the most reliable. Felt-tips can bleed on paper and dry out if the pen sits in one spot for too long Start with a short test plot a small shape first to calibrate your Z height before committing to a full design Line density matters lower density (higher number on the slider) = fewer lines = faster plot and less ink bleed. Higher density looks more solid but takes much longer to plot The settle time setting (default 120 ms) adds a brief pause after every pen up/down move. This is the main fix for random stray lines on the paper if you see faint marks between strokes, increase it to 150–250 ms Mirror X or Y if your plot comes out flipped Saving your settings In the Pen tab, click Save profile + handwriting to file to save all your pen settings, printer choice, and your custom drawn handwriting alphabet to a single .json file. Load it again any time even on a different device with the load button. Questions, problems, and ideas for future versions If something does not work, you have a question about the setup, or you just want to share your results feel free to leave a comment on this MakerWorld page or send me a message directly through MakerWorld. I am happy to help where I can, though keep in mind this is a hobby project and responses may not always be instant. If you have ideas for features you would like to see in a future version, I would love to hear them. BambuPlot is actively being worked on and new features get added regularly. Things on the radar include better SVG import, more letter styles, and improved multi-layer support. If there is something specific you need for your use case, suggest it in the comments the best ideas from the community are what shape where this goes next. BambuPlot is a fan-made tool and is not affiliated with Bambu Lab. Pen holder designs are not included search MakerWorld or Printables for a mount that fits your specific printer model. Always run a dry pass before plotting on good paper. Use at your own risk.
